ackMode: When the consumer acknowledges a message: auto acknowledges on delivery, manual only after processing succeeds. Manual mode gives you redelivery on failure but keeps the message held longer.
acks: How many replicas must confirm a write before the producer treats it as successful: 0 waits for nobody, 1 for the leader only, all for the entire ISR. More durability means higher publish latency.
activeSeries: The count of unique time series (a metric plus its label set) that the database keeps active. It is the main driver of memory and storage volume: the wall here is cardinality, not RPS.
activeSessions: How many user sessions live in the store at the same time, as a count. Together with session size and TTL it determines the memory footprint you need.
aggregationMs: The time in milliseconds the aggregator spends assembling a response from downstream call results. It adds directly to service time, on top of waiting for the calls themselves.
alarmThreshold: The utilization ρ level, a share from 0 to 1, above which the probe flags a node as overloaded. 0.9 is the usual threshold: past it the queue grows faster than the load.
alertThresholdMessages: How many messages must pile up in the DLQ, as a count, before it counts as alert-worthy. It separates a systematic processing breakage from one-off failures.
algorithm: The rule the block decides by: for a load balancer, how a backend is picked (round-robin, least-conn); for a rate limiter, what shape of burst is considered acceptable (token-bucket, sliding-window).
alwaysConnected: Whether the device holds a persistent connection instead of reconnecting for every send. Persistent sessions load the gateway with connections and memory rather than with RPS.
anycastPops: The count of anycast points of presence the service is spread across. More PoPs means lower network latency to the nearest one and better DDoS resilience.
asyncInserts: Whether the server buffers small inserts before writing them to disk. It reduces the number of parts and the merge load, at the cost of a window in which acknowledged data is not yet visible to queries.
authLatencyMs: The service-time surcharge in milliseconds for verifying a request's credentials. Local JWT validation costs a fraction of a millisecond; network introspection costs single-digit to tens of milliseconds.
authMode: How a request's credentials are verified. Local JWT validation is almost free, while introspection or a session lookup adds a network call to every request plus an external dependency.
autoSuspendMin: How many idle minutes the compute cluster waits before shutting down. A short value saves credits but pays for warm-up more often on sparse queries.
autoscale: Adjusts the instance count to the current load within the min/max bounds. With autoscaling off the pool is fixed and every spike turns into queueing and errors.
autoscaleMax: The upper bound on the instance count, as a count, that the autoscaler will not go above. This is exactly what becomes the real capacity ceiling during a load spike.
autoscaleNodes: Whether the cluster adds new nodes when there is no room left for pods. Without it, growth in replica count hits podsPerNode rather than the service's own quotas.
autoscaleTargetUtilization: The target utilization ρ the autoscaler holds, a share from 0 to 1: instances = λ·S/(concurrency·target). Typically 0.6-0.7; a higher value is cheaper but leaves less headroom for spikes.
availability: The availability of a single instance of the block, as a share from 0 to 1. Combined with redundancy and failover it yields the availability of the whole Flow path and the error budget; typically 0.99-0.99999.
avgFileSizeMb: The average file size in the store, in MB. It determines the block count and the namenode metadata volume — many small files inflate metadata far more than the data itself does.
avgObjectKb: The average size of a cached object, in KB. It converts RPS into bytes, which means egress, traffic cost, and how many objects fit in the cache.
avgObjectSizeMb: The average object size in the store, in MB. With the object count it gives the stored volume; with RPS it gives traffic and the split between per-operation charges and per-GB charges.
avgRequestKb: The average size, in KB, of a request leaving the client. Together with RPS it gives inbound bandwidth and feeds the network capacity limiter at every hop.
avgResponseKb: The average size, in KB, of a response to the client. It is the main input to egress and its cost — usually an order of magnitude larger than the request, so it is what drives the bill.
azSpread: The count of availability zones the instance pool is spread across. At 1, losing a single AZ takes the whole block down and it is flagged as a SPOF.
backend: Which store holds the block's state. Redis gives minimal latency, quorum stores give reliability at the price of RTT, and a relational database gives durability at the price of throughput.
backingStore: Where the limiter counters live. Local is fast, but the limit is counted per instance separately; Redis is exact and global, but adds a network RTT to every request.
backlogRows: How many rows, as a count, have piled up in the outbox table awaiting publication. Together with publish lag it sets the throughput the publisher needs and the size of the table itself.
backupCount: How many synchronous copies of each partition the grid keeps, as a count. Each copy multiplies write cost and memory usage, but survives the loss of a node without losing data.
bandwidthGbps: The available bandwidth of the read or transfer path, in Gbps. It yields scan time and the network capacity limiter, which often binds before CPU does.
batchMs: How many milliseconds the producer accumulates messages before sending them as a batch. A wider window raises throughput and compression efficiency, but adds directly to publish latency.
batchSize: How many records, as a count, are processed or transferred per operation. It amortizes per-call overhead, but increases the latency of an individual record and the memory held for the batch.
bitrateKbps: The bitrate of a single media stream, in kbps. Multiplied by the number of forwarded streams it gives the server's egress, which usually caps the number of rooms before CPU does.
blockCacheGb: The block cache size per region server, in GB. The more hot data fits in memory, the fewer reads go down to the distributed filesystem.
blockSizeMb: The block size, in MB, that a file is split into in the distributed filesystem. A large block relieves namenode memory pressure, but parallelizes reads more coarsely.
bookies: The count of segment storage nodes (BookKeeper), separate from the brokers. It sets the total disk available for retention and the write throughput.
botScore: The bot-scoring threshold, a share from 0 to 1, above which a request is treated as automated and blocked. A lower threshold means more false positives on real users.
bounceRate: The share from 0 to 1 of emails returned as undeliverable. It generates retries, eats part of the gateway's throughput, and damages sender reputation.
breakdown: Whether to show cost broken down by line item (compute, storage, egress, requests) instead of a single total. The breakdown makes it clear what is actually the most expensive.
brokers: The count of brokers in the cluster. It multiplies write throughput and the disk available for retention, but does not lift the consumer parallelism ceiling — partitions set that.
bucketCount: The count of buckets in the cluster. Each bucket gets its own memory quota, so this number splits the shared RAM pool across independent data sets.
buckets: The count of buckets in the latency histogram. More buckets show the tail of the distribution in finer detail, but the picture gets noisier when samples are few.
bufferPoolGb: The size of the database's in-memory page cache, in GB. If the working set does not fit, reads go to disk and service time grows 5-20×.
burst: How many requests above the limit, as a count, may be let through at once. This is the depth of the token bucket: it smooths short spikes without returning 429.
burstCredits: The accumulated throughput reserve, as a count, that the filesystem can spend above its baseline bandwidth. When credits run out, throughput drops to baseline — a sudden degradation with no growth in load.
burstiness: The squared coefficient of variation of arrival intervals c_a²: 1 is a Poisson stream, 2-4 is noticeably bursty, 8+ is a thundering herd. It multiplies queue waiting time directly.
bytesPerSample: How many bytes one compressed sample takes on disk. Typically 1.7-3 bytes for a TSDB; it multiplies by the number of active series and the scrape frequency.
bytesScanned: The volume of data, in bytes, that one query pulls from storage. Divided by bandwidth it gives execution time — exactly what partitioning and columnar formats shrink.
bytesScannedPerQuery: How many bytes a single query reads. Under scan-based billing this is a direct cost line, so partitioning and clustering pay for themselves immediately on the bill.
cacheBusting: The share from 0 to 1 of bot requests that deliberately bypass the cache with unique URL parameters. Every one of them hits the origin directly, skipping all perimeter protection against load.
cacheGb: The size of the graph's in-memory page cache, in GB. On traversals of depth 3 and deeper, a miss at each hop multiplies query latency.
cacheHitRatio: The share from 0 to 1 of requests served at the edge without going to the origin. Every percent of misses adds a percent of traffic at origin-egress prices — visible straight on the bill.
cacheSizeGb: The proxy's cache size, in GB. Together with the object size it determines how many keys fit, and through that the expected hit ratio and the load on the origin.
cacheSizeMb: The size of the database's page cache inside process memory, in MB. Anything that does not fit is read from disk and paid for in IOPS on every miss.
cacheableShare: The share from 0 to 1 of client requests that can be served from cache at all. It is the upper bound on the entire benefit of a CDN or caching proxy, however large the cache is.
callMode: How the block calls its dependencies: sequential adds up their latencies, parallel takes the maximum. Parallel is faster, but the p99 tail is amplified by the number of branches (tail at scale).
capacityMode: How the table's capacity is billed: provisioned fixes the purchased RCU/WCU and throttles anything above the limit, while on-demand scales itself but costs more per unit.
cardinalityAlarm: The active-series count threshold beyond which cardinality is considered explosive. It is used to estimate the memory required and to warn about badly chosen labels.
cellCount: The count of cells in the geo index. Together with the record size it determines index volume, while the granularity of the split determines how many cells a radius query walks.
changesPerSec: The stream of changes captured from the source log, in changes per second. If it exceeds the connector's throughput, lag grows linearly and the source WAL stops being released.
channels: How many delivery channels (push, email, SMS) a single event goes out through, as a count. A direct multiplier on provider load and on the cost of one notification.
checkpointIntervalSec: How often, in seconds, the operator persists its state. Frequent checkpoints cut throughput with barriers; rare ones increase how much has to be replayed after a failure.
chunkIntervalHours: The time interval, in hours, that the hypertable is split into. A query reads as many chunks as its range covers, so small chunks make long windows more expensive.
cidr: The subnet's address space. It determines how many IPs are available to pods and instances: exhausting the range stops scaling just as effectively as running out of CPU.
circuitBreaker: Whether calling traffic to a degraded dependency is cut off. An enabled breaker zeroes out retry amplification and turns a slow failure into a fast one.
circuitBreakerErrorThreshold: The error share from 0 to 1 at which the breaker opens. A lower threshold triggers protection sooner, but raises the risk of cutting off a healthy dependency because of a random spike.
circuitBreakerResetSec: How many seconds an open breaker waits before letting probe traffic through. Too short a period sends load back to a dependency that has not cooled down and knocks it over again.
clientCache: Whether the client caches values locally. With a cache a request costs one lookup instead of evaluating every flag, but updates arrive delayed by the poll interval.
clientRttMs: The round-trip latency, in milliseconds, from the client to the perimeter. It enters every request and is multiplied by the number of RTTs in the TLS handshake — often the largest single term in p50.
clients: The count of external API consumers. Together with per-client RPS it gives the total flow, and together with the quota it determines who gets throttled during a spike.
clockSkewRisk: The probability, as a share from 0 to 1, that clocks drift apart between generators. For time-based IDs this is the risk of broken monotonicity and collisions, which you pay for by waiting.
clusterHashSlots: How many hash slots the cluster's key space is divided into. Slots are distributed across shards and set the granularity of rebalancing when a node is added.
clustering: Whether the table orders data by clustering keys. It lets the engine prune unnecessary blocks during a scan and directly reduces the billed read volume.
code: The identifier of a region or zone, for example eu-west-1. It sets the geography, and through it the cross-region RTTs in the latency model and the price multiplier.
codec: The codec of the output stream. H.265 and AV1 give a lower bitrate and cheaper egress, but cost several times more CPU per encoded frame.
coherenceRisk: The probability, as a share from 0 to 1, that copies in different processes diverge. An in-process cache has no shared invalidation — that is the price of zero network latency.
coldStartMs: The initialization time, in milliseconds, of a new function instance. It is amortized by the cold-start share: S = serviceTimeMs + coldStartMs × coldStartShare.
coldStartShare: The share from 0 to 1 of invocations that hit a cold start. Around 0.02 with steady traffic, and noticeably higher with sparse, sawtooth, or sharply growing invocation patterns.
columnsScannedPerQuery: How many columns a typical query reads, as a count. Its ratio to the total column count sets the fraction of the table actually pulled from disk — that is the whole point of columnar storage.
columnsTotal: The total count of columns in the table. It is the denominator of the scan fraction: the wider the table, the bigger the win from reading only the columns you need.
commitConcurrency: How many transactions a node commits at the same time, as a count. Together with the quorum RTT and commit-wait it sets a write ceiling that adding read replicas will not cure.
commitServiceMs: The time, in milliseconds, of one commit into the table metadata. It is divided across the batch size, so frequent small commits are the main drag on table formats over object storage.
compaction: The merge mode for small files: none lets them pile up and kills reads, scheduled merges them in batches, and continuous keeps the data in shape at the price of constant resource use.
compactionSlots: How many merge tasks run in parallel, as a count. If their throughput falls short of the write stream, the file count grows and every scan gets more expensive.
compactionStrategy: How SSTables are merged: STCS is cheaper on writes, LCS gives predictable reads at the price of write amplification, and TWCS is designed for data with TTL and time-based windows.
compression: Whether to compress data in transit or at rest, and with which codec. It saves bandwidth and disk, but adds CPU on both sides — zstd compresses tighter, lz4 costs less.
compressionAfterDays: After how many days a chunk is converted to compressed form. Recent data stays uncompressed for write speed, while older data shrinks several times over on disk.
compressionRatio: How many × smaller the stored data is than the raw data. It divides the storage growth estimate: 1 means no compression, 3-5 for row engines, 8-15 for columnar stores and logs.
concurrency: How many tasks the block processes at the same time, as a count. By Little's law capacity = concurrency / time per task, which makes this the main lever on throughput.
concurrencyControl: How the block guards concurrent changes to the same key: none loses updates silently, optimistic turns a conflict into a retry, and pessimistic turns it into lock waiting and serialization on that key.
concurrencyPerInstance: How many requests one instance serves at the same time — threads, workers, or event loop slots. By Little's law capacity = instances × concurrency / service time.
concurrentConnections: How many connections are held open at the same time, as a count. On a push gateway it is connections and the memory behind them, not RPS, that binds first.
conflictResolution: What happens when the same key is written concurrently from different places. LWW silently loses about half of the conflicting writes; CRDT and single-writer-per-key lose nothing, but each pays its own price.
connectionDrainSec: How many seconds the load balancer gives a departing backend to finish its open requests. A short value tears down live requests on every deploy.
connectionPooler: The type of pooler in front of the database. It multiplies the connection ceiling: none ×1, pgbouncer-session ×2, proxy-managed ×5, transaction-pooling ×10 — and it is often what lifts the connections limiter.
connectionsPerInstance: How many connections a single gateway instance holds, as a count. Typically 50,000-200,000; together with the total connection count it determines how many instances you need.
connectionsPerQuery: How many connections a single query occupies, as a count. A transaction made of several round trips holds its connection longer and cuts connection-bound capacity by the same factor.
connectionsPerRequest: How many new outbound connections one request creates, as a count. With keep-alive it is a fraction of one; without it, the NAT gateway's port pool drains quickly.
consistencyModel: The strongest read guarantee the block is capable of giving at all, from linearizable down to eventual. It is an upper bound: below it, replication and read routing take over.
consumerGroups: How many independent groups read the same stream, as a count. Each group reads every message, so this is a direct multiplier on the broker's outbound traffic.
consumersPerGroup: How many consumers are in a group, as a count. They only help up to the partition count — extras sit idle; the number of lanes also governs whether processing order is preserved.
contentionRate: The share from 0 to 1 of attempts that hit a lock already held. Multiplied by the hold time, it turns a distributed lock into a hidden throughput limiter.
controlPlaneCostMonth: The fixed monthly charge for the cluster's control plane, independent of node count. It is a noticeable line item only on small clusters with few nodes.
cores: The total count of cores allocated to the job. Together with the processing window and per-core throughput it determines whether the batch makes its deadline.
costMultiplier: How many × more expensive resources in this region are than the base price list. It multiplies the compute line for every node inside the region — cheap geography shows up straight on the bill.
costPerCall: The price of a single call to the external service. At high RPS even fractions of a cent become the biggest cost line, which is why caching pays off faster than optimizing code.
costPerCoreHour: The price of one core-hour. It multiplies by the core count and by the length of the processing window — a stretched window on a small cluster costs the same as a short one on a big cluster.
costPerCredit: The price of one compute-cluster credit. Together with the warehouse size and its running time it gives the whole bill: an idle warehouse that was never suspended costs exactly as much as a working one.
costPerGatewayHour: The hourly charge for a single gateway, independent of traffic. It comes on top of the charge for processed GB, so extra gateways are expensive even with no load.
costPerGb: The price per GB passing through the gateway or a cross-AZ / cross-region link. Typically $0.01-0.02 between AZs and from $0.02 between regions, in each direction.
costPerGbEgress: The price per GB going out to the internet. On media traffic this is usually the biggest line on the bill — and exactly what a CDN with a high hit ratio saves on.
costPerGbIngest: Price of ingesting one gigabyte of telemetry, in dollars per GB. It multiplies the daily volume measured after sampling and compression; for logs and traces ingest is usually more expensive than the storage that follows.
costPerGbMonth: Price of storing one gigabyte for a month, in dollars. It multiplies the final volume including indexes, replication and compression, so every replica multiplies this line of the bill; typical values range from 0.004 for a cold archive to 0.25 for managed storage.
costPerGbMonthOffload: Price of storing one gigabyte for a month in the offload tier that old segments are moved to, in dollars. It is usually 4-5 times cheaper than broker disks, so the earlier data is offloaded, the lower the final retention bill.
costPerGbProcessed: Charge for every gigabyte of traffic that passes through the node, in dollars per GB. It is computed over the combined volume of requests and responses; expect around 0.006 for L4 load balancing and 0.045 for NAT and cross-zone traffic, and at large volumes this line overtakes the hourly instance charge.
costPerGbRetrieval: Price of retrieving one gigabyte from a cold archive, in dollars per GB, paid on top of storage on every restore. This is exactly what makes an archive cheap to store in and expensive to read from regularly.
costPerGbSecond: Price of one GB-second of function execution, in dollars: memory in gigabytes multiplied by duration in seconds. It is on the order of 0.0000166, so doubling the allocated memory doubles the cost of the same invocation even if it does not get any faster.
costPerHostMonth: Charge per monitored host per month, in dollars. It multiplies the number of hosts under observation and forms the base part of the APM bill, on top of which metrics and log ingest are added.
costPerInstanceHour: Price of renting one instance or node per hour, in dollars. It multiplies the number of instances and the hours they run per month; typical values range from 0.03 for a light node to 3 for a large database node.
costPerMessage: Price of delivering one message through a push, SMS or email provider, in dollars per message. It multiplies the notification stream measured after fanout, so with a fanout of 20 a single event costs 20 times more.
costPerMillionCpuMs: Price of a million milliseconds of edge function CPU time, in dollars. Together with cpuMsPerRequest it gives the compute part of the bill: heavy per-request logic costs more than the invocation itself.
costPerMillionGet: Price of a million object read operations (GET), in dollars. With small objects it is the operation count, not the gigabytes, that becomes the main line of the object storage bill.
costPerMillionInvocations: Price of a million function invocations, in dollars, regardless of how long they run. It adds to the GB-second cost, and for very short functions it is the dominant part of the bill.
costPerMillionIo: Price of a million I/O operations against distributed storage, in dollars. It multiplies read and write IOPS, so inefficient queries that touch many pages hurt the bill more than the size of the database does.
costPerMillionPut: Price of a million write operations (PUT), in dollars, usually an order of magnitude more expensive than GET. It makes uploading many small objects noticeably pricier than a single large upload of the same volume.
costPerMillionQueries: Price of a million DNS queries against the zone, in dollars. It is computed from the resolve stream, which itself depends on TTL and the resolver cache hit share: the lower the TTL, the more queries and the higher the bill.
costPerMillionReads: Price of a million read operations (RCU units), in dollars. It multiplies the read stream adjusted for item size, since large items consume several units per operation.
costPerMillionRequests: Price of a million requests or operations against the service, in dollars. It multiplies RPS converted into a monthly volume; the working range is 0.014-3.5, and at high RPS this is often the largest line of the bill.
costPerMillionWrites: Price of a million write operations (WCU units), in dollars, usually 4-5 times more expensive than reads. Every secondary index duplicates the write, so GSIs multiply this line of the bill.
costPerNotification: Price of one alert delivered to an on-call engineer (SMS, phone call, push), in dollars per notification. It multiplies the number of rule firings per month, including the noisy alerts that nobody ever fixes.
costPerPublicIpHour: The hourly charge for one public IPv4 address on the gateway, in dollars. It is billed per address per gateway regardless of traffic: addresses raise the port ceiling, and the bill grows linearly with them.
costPerSeatMonth: Charge per on-call seat per month, in dollars. It multiplies the size of the on-call rotation and does not depend on traffic volume, so it is the fixed part of the alerting bill.
costPerShardHour: Price of renting one stream shard per hour, in dollars. The shard count is dictated by the required throughput, so this parameter turns peak MB/s into a fixed monthly bill.
costPerStateTransition: Price of one orchestrator state transition, in dollars per transition. It multiplies the number of steps in the workflow: at the same volume an 8-step saga costs 8 times more than a single-step one.
costPerTbMonth: Price of storing one terabyte for a month, in dollars. It differs from costPerGbMonth only in the scale of the unit: 23 dollars per TB is roughly 0.023 dollars per GB.
costPerTbScanned: Price of scanning one terabyte of data with a query, in dollars. You pay for the bytes read, not the bytes returned, so partitioning and selecting only the columns you need cut this line several times over.
costPerThousand: Price of a thousand sent emails, in dollars. It multiplies the message stream, and resends after bounces and retries count as separate emails.
costPerThousandSeries: Price of a thousand active time series per month, in dollars. It multiplies cardinality: one extra high-cardinality label multiplies both the series and the bill, regardless of RPS.
costPerTransaction: External provider fee per transaction, in dollars per operation (0.029 is the fixed part of a typical rate). It multiplies the payment stream and usually dominates the infrastructure cost of this block.
cpuCores: Number of CPU cores on a single instance or node, count. Together with the instance count and the CPU share per request it sets the node's throughput ceiling; typical values are 2-32, with a limit of 192.
cpuCoresPerPop: Number of CPU cores in a single point of presence (PoP), count. Multiplied by popCount it gives the total compute budget of the edge layer and the network-wide ceiling on cpuMsPerRequest.
cpuMsLimit: Hard limit on CPU time per invocation, in milliseconds: once it is exceeded, execution is aborted with an error. Working values are 10-50 ms, and this is a CPU budget rather than a network timeout, so waiting for responses does not count against it.
cpuMsPerRequest: How many milliseconds of CPU time a single function invocation consumes. The realistic range is 1-30 ms; this parameter drives PoP capacity, the compute part of the bill, and the headroom left before cpuMsLimit.
cpuOverheadPercent: CPU overhead of the sidecar proxy, as a percentage of the service's own consumption. Typically 5-30 percent: the mesh gives you mTLS, retries and telemetry at the price of extra instances under the same traffic.
cpuPerStream: How many CPU cores a single media stream consumes, as a fraction of a core (0.01 is one hundredth of a core per stream). The working range is 0.005-0.05; together with the number of participants it determines how many rooms one node can carry.
cpuShare: What share of the service time is real CPU work, a share from 0 to 1; the rest is waiting on network and disk. At 0.15 a 20 ms request occupies a core for only 3 ms, so one core handles far more requests than 1/serviceTime; the working range is 0.05-0.6.
creditsPerHour: How many credits a running virtual warehouse burns per hour, count per hour: every size step doubles the burn (XS is 1, S is 2, M is 4). It multiplies the credit price and the time the warehouse stays up before auto-suspend.
crossRegionReplication: Enables asynchronous replication of objects to another region (yes/no). It doubles the billable storage volume and adds cross-region traffic charges, but the design survives the loss of an entire region.
crossRegionRttMs: Network round-trip between regions, in milliseconds. Realistic values are 30-150; a distributed database pays this RTT at least once per quorum commit, so the parameter sets the floor on write latency.
crossShardQueryShare: Share of queries that have to hit several shards at once, a share from 0 to 1. Working values are 0-0.2: such a query waits for the slowest shard and breaks linear scaling, so even 0.1 noticeably raises p99.
customMetrics: Number of custom metrics, that is unique time series sent to APM, count. It is billed per thousand through costPerThousandSeries and grows multiplicatively with every new dimension.
dataResidency: Data localization requirement: none means no constraints, gdpr means storage within the EU, local-only and strict mean inside a single country or region with no export. It constrains where you may replicate and where traffic may be moved on failover.
databaseSizeMb: Full size of the database file, in megabytes. It is compared against the page cache size: while the database fits into cacheSizeMb reads come from memory, and beyond that every miss costs a disk access.
datasetGb: Volume of data processed by a single batch job run, in GB. The working range is 10-500000; divided by cluster throughput it gives the length of the processing window.
dau: Number of unique daily active users, count. Together with sessions per user and requests per session it is the starting point of the whole model, since average and peak RPS for the entire design are derived from it.
dedicatedLink: A dedicated link instead of the public internet (yes/no). It gives predictable latency and bandwidth without jitter, but costs a fixed subscription fee regardless of the actual traffic.
delayDistribution: How delayed tasks are spread over time: flat means evenly across the whole horizon, exponential means most of them fire soon, long-tail means many tasks land on far-off dates. It determines whether the firing stream stays smooth or collects into a spike.
delaySec: Delay before a message becomes visible to the consumer, in seconds. It adds to the end-to-end latency and keeps a constant backlog of delayed messages in the system equal to RPS multiplied by delaySec.
deliveryLagSec: Average delay between queueing an email and its actual delivery, in seconds. Realistically 1-60; it determines how many emails are in flight at once and how quickly a user gets a confirmation code.
deliveryTimeoutMs: How long to wait for a subscriber's response before treating the delivery as failed, in milliseconds. Working values are 1000-10000: a large timeout keeps workers tied up by slow consumers and eats into delivery concurrency.
deviceCount: Number of connected devices, count. Together with the reporting interval it sets the telemetry stream: 500000 devices at a 60 second interval produce roughly 8300 RPS.
dimensions: Dimensionality of the embedding vector, count of numbers in one vector. Realistic values are 128-1536; index size and the cost of a single comparison grow linearly, so 1536 versus 768 means twice the memory and twice the search cost.
diskFetchMs: Cost of fetching a document from disk when it is not in memory, in milliseconds. Realistically 1-10 ms against fractions of a millisecond on a cache hit, and this penalty is what shapes p99 once the working set no longer fits in memory.
diskGb: Size of the node's disk volume, in GB. It caps how much data or accumulated messages the node can hold before failing, and it multiplies directly by the storage price per GB per month.
diskGbPerBookie: Disk capacity of a single bookie node, in GB. Multiplied by the number of bookies and divided by replicationFactor it gives the usable capacity, which is what caps the maximum achievable retention.
diskGbPerBroker: Disk capacity of a single broker, in GB. Together with the broker count and replicationFactor it determines how many hours of retention actually fit at the current write stream.
diskSizeTb: Capacity of a single disk, in terabytes. It multiplies disksPerNode and the node count, and the usable volume is what remains after the overhead of the erasure coding scheme.
disksPerNode: How many disks sit in one node, count. It drives both the total raw capacity and the I/O parallelism, and there must be enough disks to spread erasure coding shards across different nodes.
distKey: How rows are distributed across nodes: key means by column value, which keeps joins on that column local, even means round-robin, all means a full copy of the table on every node, auto leaves it to the engine. A poor key produces data skew and a network shuffle on every join.
diurnalPattern: Shape of the daily load profile: flat means level around the clock, business means a peak during working hours, evening means an evening peak, global means spread across time zones. It sets the peak-to-average ratio, that is how much headroom the capacity has to be built for.
dkimSigning: Whether outgoing emails are signed with a DKIM key (yes/no). It adds a few milliseconds of cryptography per email, but without the signature the share landing in spam rises sharply.
dlqEnabled: Whether a dead letter queue is enabled, a separate queue for messages that have exhausted their retries (yes/no). Without it such messages are either lost or loop forever, occupying consumers and blocking the rest of the processing.
docCount: Total number of documents in the index, count. Together with document size and the index bloat factor it gives the storage volume and the memory required for the index structures.
docSizeKb: Average size of a single document, in kilobytes. It multiplies the document count and the index bloat factor, since text takes more space in the index than in the source.
docsPerSec: Indexing stream, documents per second. The realistic range is 100-50000; it determines the load on the indexer and, together with the refresh interval, how far search lags behind the source data.
documentCount: Number of documents in the collection or bucket, count. Together with document size it gives the data volume from which the working set, the required memory and the storage cost are derived.
documentSizeKb: Average document size, in kilobytes. It affects both the storage volume and how many documents fit into a node's memory: large documents push the working set out of cache faster.
downsampleAfterDays: After how many days metrics are downsampled to a coarser resolution, in days. Everything older takes several times less space and is cheaper to keep, but the detail is lost irreversibly.
downstreamCallMs: Average latency of a single call to a downstream service, in milliseconds. Realistically 2-300; in sequential mode it adds up across all calls, while in parallel mode the slowest call determines the total.
downstreamCalls: How many downstream service calls the aggregator makes per incoming request, count. The working range is 2-12: this multiplier propagates the incoming RPS down the graph and hurts p99 through the slowest-call effect.
drainOnFailover: Whether to wait for in-flight requests to finish when switching regions (yes/no). Draining removes the error spike during a planned failover at the price of a slower switch.
drainTimeoutSec: How long to wait for active connections to finish when taking a region out of rotation, in seconds. A larger value means fewer aborted requests, but a longer switch and a higher resulting RTO.
durabilityNines: Declared storage durability in nines: 11 means 99.999999999 percent, that is an annual object loss probability on the order of 10 to the power of minus 11. It indirectly sets how many copies the storage keeps and across how many zones.
durabilityRisk: Probability of losing the most recently acknowledged writes when a node restarts after a crash, a share from 0 to 1. Realistically 0-0.1 depending on the persistence mode: asynchronous fsync is faster but widens the loss window.
durationSec: Length of the load test run, in seconds. It determines whether the system has time to warm its caches and let autoscaling react: a short run measures a cold start rather than the steady state.
edgeCount: Number of edges (relationships) in the graph, count. It is usually an order of magnitude larger than the node count and it is what drives storage volume and traversal cost, since every extra hop of depth multiplies the number of edges read.
edgeLatencyMs: Response latency from the nearest edge node on a cache hit, in milliseconds. Realistically 10-30 ms against tens or hundreds when the request goes to origin, and that difference is exactly the payoff of a CDN.
egressGbps: Outbound bandwidth of a single node, in gigabits per second. For an SFU this is usually the first resource to saturate: every participant receives a copy of every other stream, so traffic grows quadratically with room size.
ejectionPolicy: What is evicted from memory when space runs out: value-only drops only the values while key metadata stays resident, full evicts the whole document. Value-only answers a key miss quickly at the price of the memory held by that metadata.
encryption: Whether traffic on the cross-region link is encrypted (yes/no). It adds a small amount of latency and CPU for termination, but virtually every data residency regime requires it.
encryptionMs: How long one encryption or decryption operation on a secret takes, in milliseconds. It adds to the service time of every access; typically 1-5 ms, which is why secrets are cached by TTL instead of being fetched on every request.
enhancedFanout: Whether each consumer gets its own read bandwidth instead of sharing the shard's (yes/no). It removes contention between consumer groups and lowers delivery latency, but it is billed separately for every consumer.
erasureCoding: Redundancy scheme of the form ec-N-M: data is split into N chunks plus M parity blocks, and ec-8-4 survives the loss of 4 disks while requiring 1.5 times the usable volume. It directly sets the storage overhead and the number of simultaneous disk failures tolerated.
errorAlarmShare: Error share threshold above which the probe flags an edge as problematic, a share from 0 to 1 (0.01 is 1 percent). It does not affect the simulation itself and only changes what the probe marks red in the report.
errorBudgetDays: Window over which the error budget for the SLO is counted, in days. With 30 days and a 99.9 percent target the budget is about 43 minutes of downtime, and that is what the design's computed reliability is compared against.
errorRate: Share of requests to the external provider that end in an error, a share from 0 to 1 (0.01 is 1 percent). It generates retries, which means extra RPS on the same link and higher p99 because of the repeated attempts.
evaluationIntervalSec: How often alerting rules are re-evaluated, in seconds. Realistically 10-300: evaluating more often detects incidents faster, but puts a higher query load on metrics and produces more noisy firings.
evaluationMs: Cost of evaluating a single rule or feature flag, in milliseconds (typically hundredths of a millisecond). It multiplies evaluationsPerRequest and so turns into a noticeable addition to the request's service time.
evaluationsPerRequest: How many flags or configuration rules are evaluated per application request, count. The working range is 3-40; without a client-side cache every evaluation becomes a separate network call to the configuration service.
eventBytes: Average size of a single audit record, in bytes. Realistically 500-4000; it multiplies the event stream and the retention period, determining the volume and cost of the immutable archive.
eventsPerSec: Stream of audited events, count per second. Together with event size and retention, which here is measured in years, it gives the resulting volume: 5000 events per second at 1.2 KB each is roughly 500 GB per day before compression.
evictionPolicy: What to do when memory fills up: lru and lfu evict rarely used keys, ttl evicts the ones closest to expiry, random evicts arbitrary ones, and noeviction returns an error instead of evicting. For a cache noeviction turns overflow into failures, while for a datastore it protects against silent data loss.
exactlyOnce: Exactly-once processing guarantee via transactional commits and checkpoints (yes/no). It rules out duplicates on restart, but raises latency and overhead compared with at-least-once.
failbackPolicy: How traffic returns to the original region after recovery: auto means automatically, manual means on a human decision. Automatic failback shortens the time spent running degraded, but risks sending load back to a region that has not caught up on replication yet.
failoverMode: How the switch to the standby region happens: auto means driven by health checks with no human involved, manual means by hand. Auto gives an RTO of tens of seconds instead of tens of minutes, while manual rules out false switches and split-brain.
failoverSec: How long the switch to standby takes after a failure, in seconds. Realistically 10-120; this is the window in which writes do not go through, and it feeds directly into RTO and annual availability.
failureProbability: Probability of an availability zone failing over the accounting period, a share from 0 to 1 (0.0001 is one chance in ten thousand). Together with azSpread it determines the design's computed availability: without a spread across zones, one zone failure takes the whole service down.
falsePositiveRate: Share of legitimate requests wrongly blocked by the rules, a share from 0 to 1. The working range is 0.0001-0.01: at a million requests even 0.001 means a thousand blocked real users.
fanout: Whether a single published message is delivered to every subscriber (yes/no). With fanout enabled the outbound stream equals the inbound one multiplied by the number of subscribers, which multiplies both the cost and the load on the receivers.
fanoutMode: How a message reaches the right connection: direct means the gateway knows which node the client is attached to, pub-sub means the broadcast goes through a broker to every gateway node. Pub-sub is easier to scale but multiplies inter-node traffic, while direct requires a connection registry.
fanoutPerEvent: How many recipients a single event spreads to, count. The working range is 1-1000: this is the outbound stream multiplier, the thing that turns a modest event stream into thousands of messages per second.
fencingTokens: Whether a monotonically increasing number is issued together with the lock (yes/no). Without it an owner stalled in a GC pause can write data after it has already lost the lock, while a token lets the storage reject such a stale write.
fieldDataCacheGb: Memory for the field data cache used by sorting and aggregations, in GB. It is taken out of the heap: too small a cache causes constant re-reads from disk, too large one creates GC pressure and pauses.
fifoThroughputLimit: Throughput ceiling of a FIFO queue, in requests per second (RPS). This is the price of strict ordering: past that point producers get throttled, and the only ways to grow further are message groups or a move to a standard queue.
fileCount: Number of files in the cluster, count. Each file's metadata lives in the NameNode's memory, so tens of millions of small files exhaust the master's memory long before the disk space runs out.
fileSizeMb: Target size of a single data file in the table, in megabytes. The working range is 64-512: small files inflate the number of object storage requests and the planning time, while large ones reduce selectivity and read parallelism.
filterPolicy: Where unwanted messages are cut off: none means every subscriber gets everything, attributes means selection by message attributes, body means selection by its content. Filtering on the broker is cheaper than delivering a message and discarding it on the subscriber side.
firingsPerRuleMonth: How many times a single rule fires per month, count. Realistically 0.1-10; multiplied by the number of rules and the price per notification it gives both the alerting cost and the load on the on-call engineers.
firstByteLatencyMs: Time to first byte of an object storage response, in milliseconds. Realistically 20-60 for cloud storage and single digits for local storage: on small objects it is this constant, not the bandwidth, that determines read latency.
flowLogsEnabled: Whether VPC flow logs are written (yes/no). They give visibility and material for investigations, but they generate a record stream proportional to the number of connections and are billed as ordinary log ingest.
format: Columnar file format: parquet or orc. Both give compression and let a query read only the columns it needs, and the choice affects the storage volume and how many bytes a query actually scans.
fsyncMs: Cost of flushing data to disk on commit, in milliseconds. Realistically 0.5-20 depending on the media and the synchronous mode: this is the floor on transaction duration and the main limiter on writes per second.
gateways: Number of NAT gateways, count. It sets the total outbound bandwidth and the port headroom, as well as the fault tolerance: a single gateway is a single point of failure for all egress in the zone.
geo: The continent where the region physically sits. It is matched against the clients' geo profile when picking the nearest entry point, and it sets the length of the cross-region hops.
geoDistribution: Where this source's traffic comes from: a single continent or global. It decides which region the client is pulled to and which network hops end up in its latency.
geoMapping: Granularity of the DNS geo table: none means no geography, continent and country map the resolver to a region, custom uses manual rules. The finer the table, the closer the region it picks.
gpuCount: Number of accelerators on one instance (count). Together with instances it gives the total GPU count, and GPUs rather than CPUs are usually what caps the capacity of such blocks.
gpuMemoryGb: Memory of a single accelerator in GB. It limits which model and which batch fit on it: weights plus activations must fit entirely, otherwise the batch has to be cut down.
gpuType: Accelerator class: t4 and l4 are cheap, a10g is mid-range, a100 and h100 are top-end. It sets inference throughput and the hourly cost.
groupBy: The breakdown the probe uses to show traffic: by operation, by edge, or by Flow. It does not affect the simulation itself, only the grouping in the probe's report.
growthPerYear: Annual load growth as a share from 0 to 1 of the current load: 0.35 means plus 35% per year. It shows how much headroom you need for the design to survive to the end of the planning horizon.
gsiCount: Number of global secondary indexes (count). Each GSI is effectively a copy of the item: it multiplies both the WCU per write and the storage volume.
hardwareAccel: Switches transcoding from a software codec to a hardware one: speed goes up several ×, but quality per bit and profile flexibility are lower.
hdfsReplication: Number of copies of a block in the HDFS layer under HBase (count). Every write goes to all replicas, so this parameter directly multiplies both write IOPS and storage volume.
healthCheck: Whether the load balancer takes unresponsive instances out of rotation. Without it traffic keeps pouring into dead backends, and one failed node becomes a failed share of all requests.
healthCheckIntervalSec: How often the backend's state is polled, in seconds. Together with the threshold it sets the failure detection time: more frequent checks mean faster failover but more overhead requests.
healthCheckSec: Health check period for endpoints in the DNS policy, in seconds. Together with the threshold and the TTL it determines how long it actually takes traffic to leave a failed region, that is, the RTO.
healthCheckThreshold: How many consecutive failed checks (count) it takes to declare a target dead. Higher is more resistant to flapping but slower to react: detection time = threshold × interval.
heapGb: JVM heap size per node in GB. It limits how many requests can be processed concurrently; above roughly 31 GB compressed pointers are disabled and the heap becomes less efficient.
heartbeatSec: Interval between keepalive pings on each connection, in seconds. It sets the gateway's background RPS even when clients are silent: more frequent pings mean more idle traffic per million connections.
hintedHandoff: Buffers writes for a temporarily unavailable replica and replays them once it returns. It reduces write loss during short outages at the cost of load on the coordinator.
hopsPerRequest: How many times a request passes through a sidecar on its path (count). It multiplies both the mesh's latency overhead and the proxy CPU consumption.
horizonYears: The horizon in years over which the probe extrapolates storage growth. The forecast is daily growth × the period; set it to the period you actually plan purchases for.
hostsMonitored: Number of monitored hosts and agents (count). APM is billed mainly per host, so this parameter directly sets the block's monthly cost.
hotKeyShare: The share from 0 to 1 of requests that lands on the single hottest key. That key lives on one shard, so the skew caps the cluster before the total operation capacity does.
hotPartitionShare: The share from 0 to 1 of traffic going into the hottest partition. RCU/WCU limits apply per partition, so the skew pushes the table into its ceiling long before the total capacity is exhausted.
hotRetentionDays: How many days logs stay in the hot, fast-query tier before moving to cold storage. It determines what share of the volume is billed at the expensive rate.
http2: Multiplexes requests over a single connection. It sharply reduces the number of TCP connections and handshakes per client, but does not noticeably reduce proxy CPU load.
idempotencyRequired: Whether the external provider requires an idempotency key. Without one, a retry after a timeout risks creating a duplicate payment or order, the classic failure of external integrations.
idempotent: Whether it is safe to process the same message twice. With at-least-once delivery retries are unavoidable, and only idempotency removes the duplicate-processing anomaly.
idleTimeoutSec: How many seconds of inactivity before a connection is closed. A short value breaks long-lived WebSocket and long polling connections; a long one keeps connection slots and NAT ports occupied.
idsPerSec: How many identifiers per second a single generator can issue. Block capacity = instances × this value, adjusted for the chosen monotonicity mode.
immutable: WORM mode: records cannot be modified or deleted before the retention period ends. It makes the audit trail provable but adds about 20% to write volume because of versioning.
includeBackups: Whether to count backup copies in the volume estimate. The real storage bill is almost always larger than the useful data, precisely because of backups.
includeReplicas: Whether to count the volume with all replicas or only the useful data. With the flag off, the probe divides the total by the redundancy factor.
indexCount: Number of secondary indexes per table or collection (count). Each index makes writes more expensive and increases storage, while speeding up only the reads it was built for.
indexExpansionRatio: How many × larger the index is than the source documents. 1.4 is typical for search across several fields; together with the replica count it gives the final on-disk volume.
indexLagSec: The delay in seconds between a document appearing and becoming visible in search. It sets the size of the uncommitted document buffer and how fresh the index looks.
indexMode: What gets indexed at ingest: labels-only indexes just the labels, which is cheap and searchable by label; full-text indexes the whole text, which is expensive but lets you grep any field.
indexOverhead: How much indexes inflate row size, as a share from 0 to 1: 0.4 means plus 40% on top of the table. The extra counts toward both total storage volume and daily growth.
indexRamGb: How much RAM in GB is reserved for the index on each node. If the index does not fit entirely, some queries go to disk and read capacity drops in proportion to the resident share.
indexServiceMs: Time in milliseconds to index one document. Weighted by the write share of the mix, it feeds into the block's overall service time, so heavy indexing slows down search too.
indexType: The ANN index structure: hnsw gives fast search at the cost of memory, ivf is more compact but has to scan more lists for the same recall.
indexedFields: How many document fields are indexed (count). It drives index bloat and ingest cost: full-text indexing of dozens of fields can cost more than the data itself.
inferenceMs: Time in milliseconds to run the model over one batch. Together with batchSize and the GPU count it sets inference throughput and the lower bound on response latency.
ingestLagSec: The delay in seconds between the application writing a line and that line being searchable. It determines how far behind the logs are while you are investigating an incident.
insertBatchRows: How many rows (count) are batched into a single insert. Large batches sharply reduce IOPS and the number of merges; small inserts are the main cause of degradation in columnar engines.
inspectionMs: Base request inspection time in milliseconds, before the per-rule cost. It adds up with the surcharge for each rule and lands entirely on the perimeter's latency.
instances: Number of instances, pods, or nodes in the pool (count). It scales both block capacity and compute cost linearly; a single instance makes the block a single point of failure.
intervalSec: The job's run interval in seconds. Together with the duration it determines whether the previous run finishes in time and how big the load spike is at start.
intraAzLatencyMs: RTT in milliseconds between nodes inside one availability zone. If quorum is reached locally, this is the value that enters commit latency, not the cross-region one.
introspectionMs: Time in milliseconds for a remote token check against the authorization server. It applies in introspection mode and is an order of magnitude more expensive than local JWT validation, and it is paid on every request.
iopsPerRead: How many disk operations (count) one read costs. It is close to zero on a page cache hit; this parameter converts the request flow into disk load.
iopsPerWrite: How many disk operations (count) one write costs. Typically 2–4 because of the WAL, indexes, and double writes, which is why the disk saturates on writes before reads.
isPrimary: Marks the region that accepts writes. The others read from replicas, so their writes travel over a cross-region hop, and replication lag turns into RPO if the primary is lost.
isolatesPerPop: How many isolates (count) live concurrently in one point of presence. Edge compute capacity = popCount × this value / handler execution time.
isolationLevel: Transaction isolation level, from read-committed to serializable. It defines which anomalies are possible at all and how much locking and transaction retries will cost.
itemCount: Total number of items in the table (count). Together with the item size and the GSI count it gives the storage volume, and through it the monthly cost.
itemSizeKb: Average item size in KB. RCU and WCU are billed in 4 KB and 1 KB blocks, so the size directly multiplies the capacity consumed by every operation.
jobDurationSec: How long a single job run takes, in seconds. If the duration exceeds the interval, runs start overlapping, and that is where the overlap policy kicks in.
journalMode: How the journal is kept: wal keeps readers from being blocked by the writer, while delete and truncate give less concurrency and more write amplification.
jwksCacheSec: How many seconds the public key set for local JWT validation is cached. Longer means fewer trips to the issuer, but a revoked key stays alive longer after rotation.
keepAlive: Whether TCP connections are reused between requests. Without keep-alive every request pays for a handshake: extra RTT and noticeable CPU spent on TLS.
keySizeBytes: Average key size in bytes. Together with the value size and per-entry overhead it sets the memory per record, and with short values the key can weigh more than the data itself.
labelsPerSeries: How many labels (count) a single series carries. Every label increases cardinality and index size, and a cardinality explosion kills a TSDB faster than the volume of data points does.
lagAlarmSec: The consumer lag threshold in seconds above which the probe considers the queue problematic. It is a backlog evaluation criterion and does not affect the simulation itself.
lagMs: Target CDC lag behind the source, in milliseconds. It sets the volume of unread WAL and the change buffer: the larger the lag, the more space you must keep on the source.
latencyMs: The latency in milliseconds that the block or the network hop adds to every request. It accumulates along the whole path: 0.3 milliseconds for an L4 load balancer versus tens of milliseconds between regions.
latencyOverheadMs: Latency surcharge in milliseconds for one pass through a sidecar. It is multiplied by the number of hops, and that is exactly the price of the service mesh's mTLS, retries, and telemetry.
latencyUs: Latency of a single block-device operation, in microseconds. 100–500 microseconds is typical for NVMe and gp3 while spinning disks are in the milliseconds; it sets the lower bound on service time.
lazyQueues: Keeps messages on disk rather than in memory. It saves the broker from OOM when a queue backs up, but noticeably increases delivery latency.
leaseCount: How many active leases with a TTL (count) the cluster holds. Each one needs periodic keepalive, so leases eat both memory and a share of write throughput.
lifecycleDays: After how many days an object is deleted or moved to a cold storage class. It caps the accumulated volume: without a lifecycle policy storage grows linearly and without end.
limitCheckPerRequest: How many limits (count) are checked per request, for example per user, per IP, and per API key. Each check is a separate operation against the backing store.
lockHoldMs: How long an acquired lock is held, in milliseconds. Together with the contention level it sets the ceiling: a single hot key passes no more than 1000/lockHoldMs operations per second.
logBytesPerLine: Average log line size in bytes. Together with the number of lines per request it gives the GB per day flowing into the logging blocks, often the biggest observability cost item.
logIngestGb: The contractual minimum billable log ingest volume per month, in GB. The bill takes the maximum of this value and the actual flow.
logLinesPerRequest: How many log lines (count) are written per request. It multiplies the log flow directly: the difference between 2 and 8 lines is a 4× difference in storage cost.
loginServiceMs: Time in milliseconds for a full login including the password check. bcrypt or argon2 hashing is deliberately slow, so login constrains capacity far more than token validation does.
longPollingSec: How many seconds a consumer waits for a message to appear within one receive call. Long polling removes empty polls and reduces both request cost and delivery latency.
lookbackWindowSec: The depth in seconds of the window each rule is evaluated over. The wider the window and the more frequent the checks, the more data points are scanned, and that is the load on the alerting engine.
manifestOverhead: The share from 0 to 1 of manifests and metadata on top of the table's data. Typically 1–3%, but with frequent small commits manifests start to dominate the file count.
materializedViews: How many materialized views (count) are recomputed on every insert. Each one is an extra write and extra volume: reads get faster at the cost of writes.
maxAckPending: How many messages (count) can be delivered to a consumer without acknowledgement. By Little's law this limit and the processing time are exactly what set the throughput ceiling.
maxConcurrency: The ceiling on concurrently executing calls or requests (count). Capacity = limit / service time; once it is hit, requests get throttled rather than queued.
maxConnections: The limit on concurrent connections (count). A database hits it before it hits the RPS limit, which is why you need a pooler; for load balancers it is hundreds of thousands of connections per instance.
maxDbSizeMb: A hard quota on database size in MB. Exceed it and etcd goes read-only until compaction and defragmentation, a classic cluster control plane outage.
maxDelayHours: The maximum delayed-execution horizon, in hours. Together with the delay distribution it determines how many jobs sit waiting at once and how much space they take up.
maxDepth: The ceiling on the number of messages in the queue (count). Together with the retention period it limits what incoming flow the queue can absorb without overflowing.
maxDurationSec: A hard limit in seconds on a single invocation. Past it the platform kills the function, so long tasks have to be split into steps or moved to workers.
maxEntries: The ceiling on the number of entries (count) in the in-process cache. The real size is the minimum of this limit and the memory limit; the lower it is, the more eviction and the lower the hit ratio.
maxEvaluationsPerSec: How many data points per second the rule engine can scan. Capacity = limit / (rules × window / interval), so widening the window cuts it proportionally.
maxGetRpsPerPrefix: The ceiling on GET requests per second for a single key prefix. You work around it by spreading keys across prefixes, the classic remedy for a hot prefix in object storage.
maxInflight: How many messages (count) are taken for processing at once and not yet acknowledged. Together with the visibility timeout it caps throughput by Little's law.
maxIngestMbs: The ingest bandwidth ceiling in MB per second. For analytics and observability this is usually what saturates first rather than RPS, because what counts there is the byte flow, not the request count.
maxLen: A cap on stream length (count of entries), with older entries trimmed. It sets both the memory the stream uses and how much consumer lag the system survives without data loss.
maxObjectSizeMb: The maximum object size in MB that the CDN will cache. Anything larger bypasses the cache and goes straight to origin, a common cause of unexpected origin traffic.
maxOpsPerSec: The ceiling on operations per second per instance or shard. It is multiplied by the instance count and divided by the number of operations needed to serve one request.
maxOpsPerSecPerNode: How many operations per second a single node sustains. Cluster capacity grows linearly with the node count as long as data and keys are evenly distributed.
maxOpsPerSecPerRegion: The ceiling on operations per second for one HBase region, the key range served by a single region server. Too few regions per table and a hot key range becomes the bottleneck.
maxPutRpsPerPrefix: The ceiling on PUT requests per second for a single key prefix. It is lower than the read ceiling, so writes to object storage hit a hot prefix sooner.
maxQps: The ceiling on resolution requests per second that the DNS service sustains. The actual load is inversely proportional to the TTL: a longer TTL means resolvers come back less often.
maxQueueDepth: How many tasks or messages (count) fit in the queue before items are dropped. A deep queue smooths spikes but turns overload into rising latency instead of an honest rejection.
maxRcuPerPartition: The ceiling on read capacity units (count) for a single partition. Together with the hot partition share it determines when the table starts throttling under an uneven key.
maxReadsPerSecPerNode: How many reads per second a single node sustains. It is a vendor figure used to compute the node count required for the target read RPS.
maxReceiveCount: How many times (count) a message can be delivered before it goes to the DLQ. Too many and a poison message loops and burns workers; too few and ordinary transient failures end up in the DLQ.
maxRetries: The ceiling on delivery retry attempts (count). Every retry is extra load on the receiver, so aggressive retries deepen the very outage they are trying to ride out.
maxRps: The vendor ceiling on requests per second for the entry point. It caps the whole design, no matter how many backends sit behind it.
maxRpsPerInstance: An explicit RPS ceiling for a single instance. It is weighed alongside capacity by workers, CPU, and connections, and the final capacity is the minimum of them.
maxSessions: The session pool limit per node (count). Sessions are expensive to create and are held by the pool, so their number caps concurrency regardless of spare CPU.
maxSpansPerSec: The ceiling on span ingest per second. One request produces dozens of spans, so the limit is divided by the spans per request, and this is where sampling saves you.
maxWcuPerPartition: The ceiling on write capacity units (count) for a single partition, three times lower than the read one. It is the first thing to constrain a table with a hot write key.
maxWritesPerSecPerNode: How many writes per second a single node sustains. It is lower than reads because of two-phase commit and replication, so a node saturates on writes first.
mbPerShardIn: Write throughput of a single shard, in MB per second. The overall limit = shards × this value; exceeding it yields ProvisionedThroughputExceeded and requires resharding.
memoryGb: Amount of RAM per instance or node, in GB (typically 4-64). It determines how much data, indexes, buffers and connection state fit in RAM: once it runs short you get spilling to disk or OOM, which sharply hurts latency and capacity.
memoryMb: Memory allocated to a single function instance, in MB (usually 128-3008). In serverless the memory size scales the CPU share and is billed as GB-seconds, so more memory means faster execution but a higher cost per second.
memoryPerConnKb: How many KB of RAM one established connection consumes: socket buffers, TLS state, session data (realistically 20-200 KB). Together with total node memory it caps the number of concurrent connections per instance.
memoryPerMillionSeriesGb: How many GB of memory are needed per million active time series, that is per million unique metric-and-label combinations (usually 2-8 GB). Multiplied by cardinality it gives the RAM requirement, so a label explosion causes OOM long before disk runs out.
memoryQuotaGb: Memory quota on a node for the document cache and metadata, in GB. If the working set does not fit the quota, some reads go to disk and p99 latency degrades several times over.
mergeThroughputMbs: Background merge rate for segments or parts, in MB per second per node (usually 50-500). If the write stream exceeds it, the number of unmerged parts grows, reads slow down and back-pressure kicks in on inserts.
messageBytes: Average size of a single message in the channel, in bytes. Multiplied by the message rate and the connection count it gives the gateway outbound traffic in megabits per second.
messageSizeKb: Average size of one message or event, in KB (typically 1-16). Multiplied by RPS it gives throughput in MB per second, topic or queue storage volume and network traffic; managed queues have a hard cap, for example 256 KB.
messagesPerConnMin: How many messages per minute travel over a single connection on average, count (realistically 1-60). It converts to total gateway RPS as the connection count multiplied by this value and divided by 60.
messagesPerEvent: How many individual emails one business event produces, count: 1 for a plain notification and dozens on fanout to all participants. A direct multiplier on SMTP load and on sending cost.
messagesPerSec: Target email send rate, messages per second (working range 50-5000). It is compared against the provider limit and the domain reputation quota: exceeding them causes queueing, growing delivery latency and throttling.
metadataOpsPerRead: How many calls to the metadata server one read operation costs, count (usually around 1). It sets the load on the NameNode, which hits its limit before the data node disks do.
metadataOpsPerWrite: How many metadata operations one write needs, such as create, block allocation and close, count (typically 2-6). Writes are more expensive than reads in metadata terms, so this multiplier is what caps the NameNode.
metric: Which quantity to colour on the heatmap: utilization, meaning node load as a share from 0 to 1, or errors, meaning the error share. It affects only the display and does not change the calculation itself.
metricsPerSec: How many metric points are written to the database per second, count per second. The main driver of write load, WAL and IOPS, and of how fast stored volume grows.
mfaShare: Share of logins that require a second factor, a share from 0 to 1 (0.25 means every fourth login). MFA adds extra round-trips and calls to an external provider, raising average login latency and load on the auth service.
minInsync: Minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a write, count (usually 2 with replication factor 3). More replicas means higher durability but also higher write latency, and losing quorum stops writes completely.
minStorageDays: Minimum billable retention period for an object in an archive class, in days (typically 90-180). Deleting earlier is still charged for the full period, so short-lived data costs more in archive than in regular storage.
mirrorOf: Identifier of the region this region mirrors; a text name, where an empty string means a standalone region. It sets the replication direction: the mirror receives a copy of the data and adds cross-region traffic and replication lag.
mode: Operating mode of the block: storage topology (standalone, sentinel, cluster), token validation method (local JWT verification, introspection, session lookup) or multi-region scheme (single, active-active and similar). The choice determines the number of network calls per request, the behaviour on node failure and the consistency model.
modelSizeGb: Size of the model weights, in GB. It determines whether the model fits in accelerator memory and how many copies fit on an instance, as well as the cold-start time spent loading weights and the hardware cost.
moduleCount: Number of logical modules inside the monolith, count (usually 5-30). It does not affect throughput directly, but it increases build and deploy time and makes later extraction of services harder.
monotonic: Whether to require monotonically increasing identifiers, yes or no. Monotonicity simplifies sorting and B-tree index inserts, but it requires synchronizing a counter or a clock and limits generator throughput.
mtls: Whether mutual TLS is enabled between services, yes or no. It gives encryption and authentication for every call at the cost of hundreds of microseconds per handshake and noticeable CPU spent on the sidecar.
multiAz: Whether to keep replicas in several availability zones, yes or no. It protects against the loss of an entire zone, but synchronous cross-zone writes add roughly 1-2 milliseconds to commit and incur cross-zone traffic charges.
multipartThresholdMb: Threshold in MB above which an object upload is split into parts. A lower threshold gives more parallelism and resilience to broken transfers, but it increases the request count and therefore the cost and the reassembly overhead.
namenodeHandlers: Number of RPC handler threads on the metadata server that serve requests, count (realistically 32-512). It caps parallelism: when handlers run short, requests queue up and file-open time grows several times over.
namenodeMemoryGb: Memory of the metadata server, in GB (realistically 16-256). The whole namespace lives in RAM, roughly 1 GB per million objects, so this value caps the number of files in the cluster, and small files burn through it fastest.
namenodeServiceMs: Average service time of one metadata operation, in milliseconds (usually 0.5-5). Together with the handler count it sets the ceiling on metadata operations per second and the latency added to every read and write.
natGatewayCount: Number of NAT gateways in the network, count. More gateways means higher total egress throughput and better resilience to a zone failure, but proportionally higher hourly cost.
natRequired: Whether private subnets need outbound internet access through NAT, yes or no. If they do, all egress goes through the gateway, which adds a charge per GB and a shared throughput ceiling.
natThroughputGbps: Throughput of a single NAT gateway, in gigabits per second (typically 5-45). It is the egress ceiling: once it is reached you get packet loss, retransmits and rising latency.
nearCache: Whether to keep a copy of hot entries inside the client process itself, yes or no. A near-cache removes the network hop and cuts read latency to microseconds, but it consumes memory on every client and creates a staleness window.
nearCacheSizeMb: Size of the local near-cache in the client process, in MB. The larger it is, the higher the hit ratio and the fewer calls into the cluster, but the more memory it takes from every client.
negativeTtlSec: How many seconds a negative DNS answer, that is NXDOMAIN, is cached, in seconds (usually 30-300). A short TTL makes new names appear faster, a long one cuts the query flow to authoritative servers when nonexistent names are being enumerated.
networkMbps: Network throughput per instance or node, in megabits per second (usually 1000-25000). It caps total traffic: if response size multiplied by RPS exceeds the limit, the node hits the network wall before it hits the CPU one.
networkProfile: Client network type: wifi, lte, nr5g or umts. It sets the baseline RTT and the available bandwidth, from a few milliseconds on 5G and Wi-Fi to hundreds of milliseconds on UMTS, and shifts end-to-end latency directly.
networkRttMs: Network round-trip to the next hop, in milliseconds: a fraction of a millisecond inside a data center and tens to hundreds of milliseconds for a mobile client. It is added to every operation, so latency-sensitive checks such as a rate-limiter call are best kept nearby.
newConnPerSec: How many new TCP connections per second the load balancer accepts, count per second. This is a limit separate from throughput: short-lived connections and TLS handshakes run into exactly this one.
nodeCostPerHour: Cost of a single cluster node, in dollars per hour. Multiplied by the node count and the running hours it forms the main compute expense line.
nodeCount: Number of vertices in the graph, count. Together with the edge count it sets the storage volume and whether the graph working set fits in memory, which directly drives traversal speed.
nodeType: Class of cluster nodes, that is whether resources skew toward CPU, memory, GPU or disk capacity. It determines the resource ratio per node and the price per hour, and therefore whether the cluster becomes compute-bound or storage-bound.
nodes: Number of nodes in the cluster, count. It scales capacity, throughput and cost linearly; quorum systems need an odd number and at least 3 nodes to survive a single failure.
noiseRatio: Share of false and useless alerts out of the total, a share from 0 to 1 (a healthy value is below 0.5). It does not affect technical capacity, but it increases the load on on-call engineers and the reaction time to real incidents.
notifyOnArrival: Whether to send a notification when a message lands in the DLQ, yes or no. It speeds up failure detection, but during a mass failure it produces a notification storm of its own.
objectCount: Number of objects in storage, count. Together with the average size it gives the total volume in GB, and on its own it drives request and metadata cost: millions of small objects cost more than the same volume held in large files.
observabilityExport: Whether the sidecar exports metrics and traces for every call, yes or no. It gives full visibility into call chains, but it adds CPU spent on the proxy and a noticeable telemetry stream into the monitoring system.
offlineSyncBurst: How many queued offline operations a client sends in one batch when connectivity returns, count. It creates a short RPS spike on top of the normal load that has to be accounted for in peak capacity.
onCallSeats: Number of responders in the on-call rotation, people (usually 3-50). It affects the alerting system subscription cost and the escalation depth, not technical throughput.
orderingScope: The scope within which message order is guaranteed: none, per-key, per-partition or global. The wider the scope, the less parallelism: global ordering effectively means one partition and cuts throughput down to a single consumer.
originLatencyMs: Response time of the origin server on a cache miss, in milliseconds. Multiplied by the miss share, that is one minus the hit ratio, it gives the main latency added by going through the CDN.
originShield: Whether an intermediate caching layer sits in front of the origin, yes or no. It collapses misses from all PoPs into a single origin request, cutting origin load and traffic at the cost of one extra network hop on a miss.
overheadPerKeyBytes: Memory overhead per key, in bytes: headers, pointers, the hash-table entry, TTL (usually 50-200). With millions of small values the overhead can exceed the payload itself, so it is added to the required RAM calculation.
overlapPolicy: What to do when the previous run of a job has not finished yet: allow starts another one in parallel, skip drops the tick, queue lines it up. It determines peak load and the risk of accumulating backlog when runs drag on.
p50Ms: Median response time of the external service, in milliseconds (100-600 is realistic for payment providers). It sets the typical call latency and, together with the number of concurrent requests, the required connection pool size.
p99Ms: Response time of the external service at the 99th percentile, in milliseconds (often 800-8000, that is several times p50). It is what timeouts are set from, and what determines how many threads and connections get stuck on tail requests.
packetLoss: Share of packets lost on a network segment, a share from 0 to 1 (0.001 is 0.1 percent, normal for the internet). Even a fraction of a percent of loss noticeably reduces effective TCP throughput and inflates the latency tail through retransmits.
parallelism: Number of parallel tasks or stream processing slots, count (working range 2-512). It is capped from above by the number of source partitions: more slots than partitions leaves tasks idle, fewer leads to growing lag.
