partialFailureMode: Behaviour when some of the backends fail: degrade returns an incomplete response, fail-fast returns an error immediately. Degradation raises observed availability, but it requires the client to handle partial data correctly.
participantsPerRoom: Average number of participants in one room, people (realistically 2-50). SFU load grows roughly quadratically with this number, since every participant has to be sent everyone else streams, and it is the main driver of CPU and traffic.
partitionKey: The field or set of fields data is distributed by across partitions and shards; specified as a text attribute name. Its cardinality and uniformity determine load skew: a poor key creates hot partitions that hit the limit of a single node.
partitionScheme: Partitioning scheme for data in the lake: none, hour, day or month. It determines how many files a query scans: hourly partitions speed up queries over short periods but create a small files problem.
partitionSizeMb: Average size of one partition or range, in MB: single to hundreds of MB for columnar partitions and 128-1024 MB for ranges in distributed SQL. Oversized partitions read slowly and rebalance painfully, undersized ones inflate metadata.
partitionStrategy: How data is laid out across nodes and regions: range by key ranges, geo-partitioned with rows pinned to the user region, global-table with a full copy in every region. It determines whether a write stays local, that is a few milliseconds, or needs a cross-region quorum of tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
partitioning: Granularity of time partitioning for the table: none, hour, day or month. Fine partitions let a query read less data, meaning it runs cheaper and faster, but they multiply small files and inflate metadata.
partitions: Number of partitions in the topic, count (working range 3-200). It caps consumer parallelism, since one partition is read by one consumer in a group; excess partitions burden brokers with metadata and lengthen rebalances.
partsPerPartition: How many data parts are allowed in a single partition, count (working range 10-300). Many parts slow reads down and lead to the too many parts error, that is inserts stop, when merging cannot keep up with writes.
pattern: Shape of the load profile: constant, ramp, spike or sawtooth. It determines what is being tested: the steady state of the system, or the reaction of autoscaling and queues to a sudden traffic jump.
payloadBytes: Payload size of a single message from a device, in bytes (typically 20-4096). With millions of devices this, together with the send rate, is what sets the entire inbound traffic and the telemetry storage volume.
payloadLimitMb: Maximum request body size the gateway lets through, in MB. Requests above the limit are rejected with a 413; a high limit requires more memory for buffering and makes attacks with large bodies easier.
peakFactor: How many times peak traffic exceeds average, a dimensionless multiplier in × (realistically 1.5-6, closer to 1 for IoT). All capacity is sized from the peak, so this factor directly multiplies the required instance count and the cost.
peeringLatencyMs: Latency of traffic passing over peering between networks, in milliseconds (inside a region usually 0.1-1). It is added to every cross-VPC call and is noticeable only on long chains that are sensitive to latency.
pendingJobs: How many deferred jobs are waiting for their trigger time at once, count. It determines the memory and disk needed for the queue and the cost of periodically selecting the jobs that are due next.
pendingLimit: Maximum number of messages taken by a consumer group but not yet acknowledged, count (working range 1000-100000). A large limit consumes memory and lengthens recovery after a consumer crash, a small one limits processing parallelism.
perInstance: Whether the cache is per-instance or shared by all instances, yes or no. A per-instance cache gives minimal latency with no network hop, but the hit ratio falls in proportion to the instance count and memory is spent on every one.
perSessionMbs: Throughput of a single user file transfer session, in MB per second (realistically 1-100). It is multiplied by the number of concurrent sessions and runs into the overall network link of the server.
percentile: Which latency percentile to show in the per-stage breakdown: p50, p95 or p99. SLO work usually looks at p99, since that is what reveals the tail latencies invisible in the median.
period: The period cost is aggregated over: hour, day, month or year. It changes only the scale of the displayed amount, not the calculation model itself.
persistence: Disk persistence mode: none is in memory only, rdb is periodic snapshots, aof journals every write, rdb-aof does both at once. The stricter the mode, the less data is lost on a crash, but the higher the disk load and the more visible the latency spikes during fork and fsync.
pipelining: Whether to send several commands in one packet without waiting for the reply to the previous one, yes or no. Pipelining amortizes RTT and raises throughput several times over, but it increases the latency of an individual command inside the batch.
podsPerNode: Maximum number of pods on a single node, count (the standard limit is 110). Together with the node count it sets the pod capacity of the cluster: high density saves nodes but runs into IP address limits and kubelet overhead.
pointsPerSec: How many metric points are written per second, count per second. The main driver of write load, WAL and compaction, and of how fast stored volume grows.
pollIntervalMs: How often a worker polls the outbox table, in milliseconds (working range 50-1000). A shorter interval cuts event publication latency, but it linearly increases the number of empty queries against the database.
pollIntervalSec: Polling interval for a source, be it a server, a job queue or configuration, in seconds. The shorter the interval, the faster changes arrive, but the higher the constant background RPS: it equals the client count divided by the interval.
popCount: Number of points of presence at the edge, count (usually 50-400). More PoPs cut RTT to the user, but they fragment the cache: the same objects get pulled from the origin into every PoP, which lowers the effective hit ratio.
portHoldSec: How many seconds a port is held after a connection closes before it can be reused, in seconds (typically 15-120). Together with the number of new connections per second it determines how many ports are occupied at once and whether SNAT exhaustion occurs.
portsPerIp: How many ephemeral ports are available per public IP, count (the practical ceiling is around 64000). Divided by the port hold time it gives the limit of new outbound connections per second for each address.
precision: Detail level of a geo-index cell, a dimensionless level from 1 to 12 (5-9 in practice). Each level shrinks the cell roughly fourfold: higher precision means fewer spurious candidates to check, but more cells to enumerate in a radius search.
prefetch: How many messages a consumer takes ahead without waiting for acknowledgement of the previous ones, count. A large prefetch raises throughput, but it worsens the balance across workers and increases the amount of reprocessing after a crash.
prefixCount: Number of prefixes, count: for a search index it is the number of unique string prefixes, which sets the in-memory structure size, while for object storage it is the number of key prefixes the load is spread over. In the second case each prefix gets its own quota of requests per second, so having few of them leads to throttling.
priorityLevels: Number of priority levels in the queue, count (1 means priorities are off, the practical maximum is around 10). A priority queue requires extra sorting, so every additional level lowers broker throughput.
processingTimeMs: Average processing time of one message or job, in milliseconds. Its inverse gives the throughput of a single worker: 100 milliseconds is 10 jobs per second per thread, and the required worker count equals RPS multiplied by the time and divided by 1000.
produceLatencyMs: Time for the broker to acknowledge a write to the producer, in milliseconds (usually 1-10 with acknowledgement from all replicas inside a region). It is added to the latency of a synchronous write and caps producer throughput without batching.
providerLimitRps: The external provider limit on the number of requests per second, RPS. Exceeding it results in 429 responses and retries, so the outbound stream has to be smoothed with a queue or a rate-limiter.
provisionedConcurrency: How many function instances to keep permanently warm, count (0 means on-demand start only). It removes cold starts for that many concurrent requests, but it is billed around the clock even at zero traffic.
provisionedIops: Provisioned disk performance, in input/output operations per second (IOPS). It is the ceiling for storage reads and writes: once it is reached the disk queue and request latency grow, and in the cloud these IOPS are billed separately from capacity.
publicIps: Number of public IP addresses on the egress NAT, count. Each one adds about 64000 ports, that is it raises the ceiling on concurrent outbound connections linearly.
publishLagMs: Delay between the transaction commit and the publication of the event to the external broker, in milliseconds (typically 100-5000). This is the window in which the data already exists in the database but subscribers do not know about it yet, and it defines the observable inconsistency between services.
publishLatencyMs: Time to acknowledge the publication of a message to a queue or bus, in milliseconds: a fraction of a millisecond for in-memory buses and 5-20 milliseconds for managed services. It is added to the latency of the synchronous write path if the producer waits for an ack.
purgeApi: Whether an API for forced cache invalidation is available, yes or no. It lets you set long TTLs and flush content on an event, raising the hit ratio without the risk of serving stale data.
pushEnabled: Whether to use push notifications instead of polling the server periodically, yes or no. Push removes background polling traffic and saves battery, but it adds a dependency on an external delivery service and its limits.
pushMode: Whether configuration changes are delivered by subscription, that is push, instead of polling, yes or no. Push applies changes within seconds and removes idle requests, but it requires holding long-lived connections to every instance.
pushdown: Whether to push filters, projections and aggregations down to the data source, yes or no. Pushdown drastically cuts the volume of bytes read and sent over the network, speeding up the query and lowering the scan cost.
quantized: Whether to use quantized weights, for example int8 or int4, instead of full precision, yes or no. Quantization shrinks the model by 2-4× and speeds up inference, lowering accelerator memory requirements at the cost of a small quality loss.
queriesPerDay: Number of queries against the warehouse per day, count per day (working range from hundreds to hundreds of thousands). Together with the volume of data scanned per query it determines the cost, since billing is per scanned byte, and the required concurrency.
queryComplexity: Class of the graph query: point-read, neighbourhood traversal, variable-depth traversal or shortest path search. Each next class is an order of magnitude more expensive, since the number of visited vertices grows exponentially with traversal depth.
queryConcurrency: How many queries run at the same time, count. It caps engine throughput: beyond this number queries queue up and the wait is added to their response time, while too high a concurrency splits memory and CPU and slows everyone down at once.
queryConcurrencyPerNode: How many search queries a single node handles at the same time, count. Multiplied by the node count it gives the total cluster throughput; exceeding it overflows the search thread pool and leads to rejected errors.
queryProfile: Typical query profile: point-read by key, range-scan, join, aggregate or full-scan. It determines how many pages are read per query, from a handful on a point-read to the whole table on a full-scan, and therefore the required IOPS and latency.
queryRadiusKm: Radius of the geographic search, in kilometers (working range 0.5-50). The number of index cells examined grows roughly quadratically with the radius, so a wide search costs substantially more than a pinpoint one.
queryRangeHours: Depth of the time window of a typical query, in hours (168 is one week, working range 1-720). It is directly proportional to the volume of chunks scanned: the wider the window, the more data is read and the more important continuous aggregates become.
queryServiceMs: Pure engine processing time for a single search or analytical query, in milliseconds, excluding queue wait. It sets both latency and capacity: at 5 milliseconds one thread sustains about 200 requests per second; typical values are 1-50 milliseconds, and heavy analytics runs into the hundreds.
queryType: Class of search query: term is an exact match on a non-analyzed field (the cheapest), match is full-text search with scoring, aggregation covers facets and aggregations over the whole set. A dimensionless choice that multiplies service time: aggregation costs several times more than term.
queueLimit: Maximum length of the queue of requests waiting for a free worker, as a count (0-1000000, practical values in the hundreds to thousands). It caps how far latency can grow under overload: anything that does not fit is dropped immediately, so overload turns into errors instead of an unbounded rise in p99.
queuePriority: Order in which the job queue is drained: fifo strictly by arrival, weighted with weights across classes, strict with hard priority for the higher classes. A dimensionless choice; it does not change overall throughput but redistributes waiting, and under strict low-priority jobs can wait indefinitely.
queueType: Queue type: standard gives virtually unlimited throughput at the cost of at-least-once delivery and possible message reordering; fifo gives strict ordering and deduplication but caps out at about 300 messages per second per group (3000 with batching). A dimensionless choice that directly bounds the computed capacity.
queues: Number of queues in the broker, as a count (1-100000). Each queue keeps its own structures in memory, and a quorum queue also maintains its own Raft quorum, so the number of queues loads broker memory and CPU more than the total message flow does.
quorumN: Total number of replicas taking part in the quorum protocol, as a count (usually 3-6, at most 12). Together with R and W it defines consistency: when R + W is greater than N a read is guaranteed to see the latest write; raising N multiplies storage volume and write work.
quorumQueues: Flag for using Raft-based quorum queues instead of classic mirrored ones. Enabling it gives predictable failover with no loss of acknowledged messages, but every message is replicated to a majority of nodes, so throughput of a single queue drops and disk usage grows.
quorumR: How many replicas must respond for a read to be considered successful, as a count (1 is the fastest, N the most consistent). A lower R reduces read latency and improves availability, but when R + W is not greater than N you risk reading stale data.
quorumW: How many replicas must acknowledge a write before it counts as committed, as a count. Raising W increases durability and write latency at the same time, since you wait for the slowest of the W replicas; the condition R + W greater than N yields strong consistency.
quotaPerDay: Daily call limit per client or API key, in requests per day (1 to 10 billion). It caps cumulative volume rather than the peak: a quota of 1000000 per day averages about 11.6 requests per second, and any burst uses it up early.
rangeRequests: Flag for HTTP Range support: whether the edge serves chunks of an object by byte range. It is needed for video and large files (seeking, resumable downloads), but it splits one object into many requests, so RPS grows for the same number of bytes transferred.
rateLimitRps: Ceiling on admitted calls, in requests per second; everything above it is dropped or queued. This is a hard cap on the block's capacity: when the incoming flow exceeds the limit, the excess traffic turns into errors rather than higher latency.
rateLimitRpsPerClient: Limit for a single client (key, token, IP), in requests per second (1-1000000). It bounds the contribution of one noisy neighbor rather than the gateway's total capacity; the overall ceiling is this value multiplied by the number of active clients.
rawGbPerDay: Volume of raw data arriving in storage per day, in GB (practical values in the hundreds and thousands). Multiplied by the retention period and divided by the compression ratio it gives storage size and cost: 2000 GB per day is about 60 TB of raw data per month.
rcu: Provisioned Read Capacity Units, as a count per second: one RCU is one strongly consistent read of an item up to 4 KB per second, or two eventually consistent reads. Items larger than 4 KB consume several RCUs, and exceeding the provisioned value causes throttling rather than a slowdown.
readFromReplica: The share of reads, from 0 to 1, that may be routed to replicas instead of the primary. The leader is offloaded by exactly this share, and for exactly this share of reads you get data that is behind by the replication lag.
readPreference: Where to send reads: primary means the leader only (strong consistency), primary-preferred means the leader with fallback to a replica, secondary means replicas only, nearest means the closest node by network. A dimensionless choice; everything except primary lowers latency and leader load at the cost of stale reads.
readReplicas: Number of read-only replicas, as a count (0-15, practical values 1-5). Each one adds roughly one instance worth of read capacity and the same amount to the bill, but write capacity does not grow at all, since it stays entirely on the primary.
readServiceMs: Pure engine processing time for a single read, in milliseconds, excluding queue and network. It determines both latency and capacity: 0.5 milliseconds allows up to 2000 reads per second per thread; an in-memory hit costs tenths of a millisecond, a miss going to disk costs single-digit to tens of milliseconds.
readWriteMix: The share of reads in the client's traffic, from 0 to 1: 1 means reads only, 0 means writes only. It splits load across two paths with different costs, since writes are not cached and go to the primary, so 0.9 versus 0.5 radically changes the database capacity required.
realtimeIngestRps: Stream of events ingested in real time, in records per second (practical values 10000-2000000). It sets the number of indexing tasks and the memory for segments not yet flushed; this stream creates no load on historical queries.
recallTarget: Target recall of approximate search, the share of true nearest neighbors the index must find, from 0 to 1 (practical values 0.9-0.99). Every extra nine is expensive: going from 0.9 to 0.99 typically multiplies the number of candidates examined, and with it query time and CPU.
recordsPerSecPerTask: How many records per second a single operator task (slot) can digest, with practical values of 1000-200000 depending on how heavy the logic is. Dividing the incoming stream by this number gives the required parallelism, and from that the core count and the cost.
recordsPerShard: Ingest ceiling for one stream shard, in records per second (a standard shard allows 1000 records and 1 MB/s). Together with the shard count it gives total ingest capacity; exceeding it returns a throughput exceeded error rather than stretching latency.
redriveDelaySec: Pause before messages are moved from the DLQ back to the main queue, in seconds (0-86400, typically 60-900). It gives the dependency time to recover: too short a delay pushes the flow back onto a service that has not cooled down, and the DLQ fills up again.
refreshAhead: Flag for proactive refresh: whether to re-read an entry before its TTL expires instead of waiting for a miss. It removes latency spikes on hot keys but creates a background stream of requests to the origin even when nobody is asking for the data.
refreshIntervalSec: How many seconds it takes for written documents to become visible to search (0.1-300). This is the near-real-time window: 1 second gives almost instant search at the cost of many small segments and constant merging, while 30 seconds is noticeably cheaper on CPU.
refreshTokenTtlSec: Lifetime of a refresh token, in seconds (2592000 is 30 days, the maximum is a year). A long TTL reduces repeat logins but proportionally increases the size of the active-session store and the window in which a stolen token still works.
regionServers: Number of region servers in the cluster, as a count (practical values 3-200). It scales read and write capacity and the total block cache size linearly; the overall number of regions is also divided among them.
regions: Number of regions the system is spread across, as a count (1-20, usually 2-3). More regions mean lower latency to the nearest one and better resilience, but a cross-region quorum adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds of RTT to every write and multiplies traffic and cost.
regionsPerServer: How many regions a single server serves, as a count (practical values 20-300). Each region holds its own MemStore, so an excess of regions eats memory and makes flushes to disk more frequent, while too few prevent the load from being parallelized.
registeredInstances: How many service instances are registered in the registry, as a count (1-1000000). It sets the catalog size, the volume of broadcast updates and the heartbeat background: 900 instances at a 10-second interval means about 90 requests per second just to keep registrations alive.
rejectMode: What to do with a call above the limit: http-429 returns an error with Retry-After, queue holds it until a slot frees up, shed drops it silently. A dimensionless choice; queue turns an overage into higher latency, while the other two turn it straight into errors.
renditions: How many quality variants (resolution and bitrate) are generated from one source, as a count (practical values 3-8). It linearly multiplies transcoding CPU and GPU, storage volume and egress: 5 renditions cost five times as much as a single track.
replicaLagMs: How far the data on a replica trails the leader, in milliseconds. It defines the inconsistent-read window: a request that reaches a replica sooner than this after a write will see the old value; typical values are 1-100 milliseconds within a zone and hundreds to thousands with asynchronous cross-region replication.
replicaLagSigma: Spread of the replication lag, a dimensionless coefficient of variation of a lognormal distribution (0.1-3, usually around 0.8). The mean says nothing about the tail: the higher the sigma, the more the p99 lag exceeds the mean and the more often stale reads happen.
replicaSetSize: How many nodes make up the replica set, as a count (practical values 3-7, always odd). It sets the election quorum: a set of 3 survives the loss of one node, a set of 5 survives two; more nodes mean costlier storage and slower writes that wait for a majority acknowledgement.
replicas: Number of extra copies of each shard, as a count (0-3, usually 1-2). Each copy adds read capacity and survival of a node failure, but it multiplies storage volume and write work by the same factor.
replicasPerShard: How many replicas there are per shard, as a count (0-5, usually 1-2). It multiplies the total node count as shards × (1 + replicas), and with it the cost and the read capacity; at 0 a node failure means losing its key range.
replication: Block replication factor, how many physical copies of each block are stored, as a count (practical values 2-3). It directly multiplies disk requirements: at 3, every terabyte of useful data needs 3 TB of raw capacity, but the cluster survives the loss of two nodes.
replicationDirection: Direction of cross-region replication: one-way means one region writes and the rest only read; bidirectional means you can write in any region. A dimensionless choice; bidirectional removes the cross-region RTT from the write path but creates conflicts that need a separate resolution strategy.
replicationFactor: How many copies of each partition or range the cluster stores, as a count (usually 3, or 5 for critical data). It multiplies storage volume and write traffic by the same factor; with quorum writes, RF 3 survives one node failure and RF 5 survives two.
replicationMode: When a write counts as committed: sync after all replicas acknowledge, semi-sync after at least one, async immediately after the leader. A dimensionless choice that directly shifts the trade-off between write latency (sync adds a full RTT to the replica) and the risk of data loss when the leader fails.
reportIntervalSec: How often a device sends a telemetry packet, in seconds (0.1-86400). It inversely sets the fleet's RPS: a million devices at a 60-second interval produce about 16700 requests per second of constant background traffic.
reprocessBatchSize: How many messages are pulled from the DLQ in one reprocessing pass, as a count (1-10000). A large batch clears the backlog faster, but replayed against a service that is not fixed yet it creates a load spike the size of the batch itself.
reprocessMode: How messages are returned from the DLQ: manual only on a human command, auto right on arrival, scheduled in batches on a timetable. A dimensionless choice; auto without a sane backoff loops poison messages forever and burns handler capacity for nothing.
requestTransform: Flag for request transformation at the gateway: rewriting paths and headers, converting the body, REST to gRPC. It requires parsing and rebuilding the payload, so it adds noticeable fractions of a millisecond and CPU to the gateway's service time, growing with the body size.
requestsPerSession: How many requests a user makes in a single session, as a count (1-10000, typically 20-60). The multiplier between sessions and load: DAU × sessions per day × requests per session / 86400 gives the average RPS.
resolveMs: Time of a full name resolution on a cache miss, in milliseconds (1-500, typically 15-40). It is paid once per connection setup and lands entirely in the p99 of a cold request; on a resolver cache hit it is effectively zero.
resolverCacheHitRatio: The share of lookups, from 0 to 1, served from the resolver cache without going to the authoritative source. It weights the average resolution latency and offloads the registry: at 0.9 only one request in ten reaches the source.
respectRobots: Flag for honoring robots.txt and its Crawl-delay directive. Enabling it cuts the crawler's actual RPS down to the rate the site permits: load on the target drops, but a full crawl stretches out over time.
responseCacheEnabled: Flag for caching responses at the gateway itself. It cuts off part of the traffic before the backends (at a hit ratio of 0.5 the load on services halves), but it returns data as old as the cache TTL and applies only to idempotent reads.
responseCacheTtlSec: How many seconds a response lives in the gateway cache (0-86400, typically 5-60). It sets both the hit ratio and the maximum age of the data served: as the TTL grows, backend load falls with diminishing returns while staleness grows linearly.
retentionDays: How long data is kept before deletion, in days (1-3650). A linear multiplier of storage volume and cost: daily volume × retentionDays / compression ratio.
retentionHours: How many hours messages stay in the broker after publication (168 is a week, 336 is two). It sets the disk volume as flow × hours × replica count, and the time budget for replay: a consumer that falls behind by more than this loses the data for good.
retentionPolicy: Horizon for automatically deleting old points: none keeps everything, while day, month or year trim to the corresponding period. A dimensionless choice that caps database growth, and with it disk usage and the scan time of long queries.
retentionYears: Retention period of the audit log, in years (1-30; regulatory requirements are usually 3-10). It directly multiplies the archive size: at 7 years that is about 2500 daily slices, which is why old data is almost always moved to a cold storage class.
retries: How many times a call is retried after an error, as a count (0-10, typically 1-3). Every attempt is extra load on an already degraded dependency: with 3 retries a failure triples outgoing traffic, so retries only make sense with backoff and for idempotent operations.
retrievalHours: How many hours pass between a restore request and the object becoming available (practical values 1-12). This is not request latency but the time to the first byte out of the archive, and it is what sets the achievable RTO when recovering from cold storage.
retrievalTier: Speed class of restoring from the archive: expedited takes minutes and is the most expensive, standard takes several hours, bulk takes 5-12 hours and is the cheapest. A dimensionless choice that changes both the time to data and the price per GB retrieved by roughly an order of magnitude.
retryBackoffMs: Base pause between retry attempts, in milliseconds (0-60000). With exponential backoff it is multiplied by the attempt number: too small a value turns retries into a storm against a downed dependency, too large a value stretches out delivery.
retryPolicy: Retry rule: none never retries, once allows a single extra attempt, idempotent-only retries safe methods, exponential-backoff makes a series of attempts with a growing pause. A dimensionless choice; retries improve observed availability but multiply load and, without an idempotency restriction, can apply an operation twice.
rollupRatio: The factor, in ×, by which pre-aggregation at ingest reduces the number of rows, a dimensionless multiplier (1 means no rollup, practical values 2-100). It divides both storage volume and the number of rows scanned: a rollup of 8 collapses eight events into one row at the cost of losing detail on the dimensions left out.
routingPolicy: Rule for picking the destination: simple round-robins, latency goes to the fastest endpoint by network, geo follows the client's geography, weighted uses configured shares, failover switches to the standby only when the primary fails. A dimensionless choice that determines network latency and how load is distributed across regions.
rowCount: How many rows are stored in the table or dataset, as a count (up to hundreds of billions). Together with the row size it gives the volume of data and indexes, and it determines whether the working set fits in memory and how many rows a query without a suitable index has to scan.
rowSizeBytes: Average size of one row or record, in bytes (typically 100-2000). It converts a row count into GB of storage and into disk read volume: a billion rows of 500 bytes each is about 500 GB before compression.
rowsIngestedPerSec: Stream of inserted rows, as a count per second (practical values 10000-5000000). It drives both table growth and the CPU spent on background merges; small frequent inserts instead of batches multiply the number of parts and the merge load at the same throughput.
rowsPerSegment: How many rows are packed into one segment, as a count (practical values 1-10 million). It sets the granularity of parallelism: small segments multiply the overhead of tracking and opening them, large ones prevent a query from being parallelized across nodes.
rpoTargetSec: Recovery Point Objective, how many seconds of recent data it is acceptable to lose when a region fails (0-86400). In practice it is the upper bound on replication lag: an RPO of 0 requires synchronous writes to two regions, that is a full cross-region RTT on every commit.
rps: Steady stream of calls from the source, in requests per second. The primary input of the whole model: this is what fanout multiplies across the downstream blocks until it hits their capacity.
rpsPerClient: How many requests per second a single integration client makes (0.01-100000, typically single digits). Multiplied by the number of active clients it gives the total incoming flow, and it is compared against the gateway's per-client limit.
rtoTargetSec: Recovery Time Objective, how many seconds the service has to come back up after a region failure (0-86400; 900 is 15 minutes). It dictates how much automation is needed: a manual switchover rarely fits into less than tens of minutes, and warming up the standby plus DNS record TTL count against this budget.
rules: Number of alerting rules evaluated on a schedule, as a count (practical values 20-5000). Each rule is a periodic query to the metrics store, so the load it creates equals the number of rules divided by the evaluation interval.
rulesCount: Number of filtering rules applied to every request, as a count (0-5000, practical values 100-800). The checks run in a chain, so the rule set adds directly to service time and grows with the size of the request body being parsed.
runtime: The service's execution runtime, a dimensionless choice that sets the concurrency model and the cost. Go and dotnet give cheap threads and low latency spread, jvm gives high throughput after warm-up plus GC pauses and slow startup, while node and python keep one thread per process and scale by adding processes.
samplesPerSec: How many individual metric values are written per second, as a count. The main driver of volume: about 2 bytes per sample after compression, so 700000 samples per second produce roughly 1.4 MB/s; the number itself works out as active series divided by the collection interval.
samplingRate: The share of events, from 0 to 1, that is actually stored: 1 means write everything, 0.1 means every tenth. It linearly divides storage volume and ingest cost, but accuracy is the price: at 0.01 rare errors simply never make it into the sample.
scale: Axis scale of the latency histogram: linear uses equal intervals, log uses logarithmic ones. A dimensionless choice that affects display only: a logarithmic scale shows both the typical values and the p99 tail at once, whereas a linear one squeezes that tail into a single bar.
scaleDownLagSec: How many seconds the autoscaler waits before removing surplus instances (0-86400, typically 300). It guards against flapping: a short window saves money, but with sawtooth load it makes you pay in cold starts over and over.
scaleUpLagSec: How many seconds pass between load rising and new instances being ready (0-3600, typically 30-120). The old instances carry all the traffic for that whole period, so this lag is what determines how deep the dip is during a sharp spike.
scanThroughputMbsPerCore: How many megabytes of compressed data per second a single core scans (practical values 50-500). Dividing the volume of scanned data by this number and by the core count gives the analytical query time.
scheduleCron: Run schedule in five-field cron format: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week; the default value means once an hour at the top of the hour. It is a text value with no units that shapes the load rather than setting its rate: jobs that coincide in time produce a synchronized spike, so runs are worth spreading out.
schedulingLagSec: How many seconds pass between a pod being created and it being ready to take traffic: scheduling, image pull, probes (0-600, typically 10-60). It adds up with the autoscaler lag, and together they set how fast the cluster really reacts to load.
scope: Scope of effect: for the rate limiter it is the key the limit is counted by (global covers the whole service, while per-user, per-ip and per-key cover an individual client); for the heatmap it is what gets highlighted (scheme means the entire scheme, subtree only the selected block's subtree). A dimensionless choice; for the limiter it decides whether traffic is capped in aggregate or every client gets its own budget.
scrapeIntervalSec: Polling period for targets, in seconds (practical values 10-60). It inversely sets the sample stream and the storage volume: moving from 15 to 30 seconds halves both, but it also halves the time resolution of graphs and the speed at which alerts fire.
segments: Total number of data segments in the cluster, as a count (practical values 1000-2000000). It determines the size of the coordinator's metadata and the cache holding their placement; each segment is a separate file that must be accounted for during query planning and opened on read.
segmentsScannedPerQuery: How many segments a single query actually scans, as a count (practical values 1-500). A direct multiplier of work: good filtering by time and partition leaves a handful, a full scan leaves thousands, and query time grows with this number.
seriesCardinality: Number of unique time series, that is combinations of a measurement and a tag set, as a count (practical values 100000-10000000). The main memory constraint in a TSDB: the series index lives in RAM, and a single high-cardinality tag such as userId blows this number up by orders of magnitude.
seriesPerQuery: How many series a typical query touches, as a count (practical values 10-10000). It multiplies the volume of points read: 1000 series over a day at a 15-second step is about 5.8 million points that have to be decompressed and summed.
serviceTimeMs: Pure time the block spends processing one call, in milliseconds, excluding queue wait. The base quantity of the model: a single worker's capacity is 1000 / serviceTimeMs requests per second, and observed latency grows as S / (1 - ρ) as utilization approaches one.
serviceTimeSigma: Spread of processing time, a dimensionless coefficient of variation (0.1 means almost constant time, 1 and above means a heavy tail). At the same mean, a higher sigma sharply increases queue wait and p99: long requests occupy workers and a tail builds up behind them.
services: Number of logical services in the registry, as a count (1-10000). Together with the instance count it sets the catalog size and the number of watch subscriptions: clients subscribe to changes by service name, so this number determines how many broadcast channels there are.
sessionDurationMin: Average length of a single session, in minutes (practical values 5-120). Through Little's law it sets the number of concurrently live sessions as new-session rate × duration, and with it the memory for state and the number of open connections.
sessionSizeKb: Average amount of data in one session, in kilobytes (practical values 1-16). Multiplied by the number of active sessions it gives the memory the store needs: 10 million sessions of 4 KB each is about 40 GB plus data-structure overhead.
sessionStore: Where session state lives: none means stateless, redis is an external cache with a sub-millisecond lookup, database is more durable but costlier in latency, cookie-jwt keeps it on the client with no store lookup at all. A dimensionless choice that sets the cost of every check and whether instant revocation is possible, which cookie-jwt does not offer.
sessionsPerUserDay: How many times a day one user starts a new session, as a count (0.1-200, typically 1-10). It links DAU to the session rate and, through requests per session, to the resulting RPS.
shardCount: How many shards the data is split into, as a count (1-4096, practical values 4-256). It scales write capacity linearly and reduces the volume per node, but a query without the shard key fans out to every shard, and then its cost grows with this number.
shardKey: Name of the field by which rows are distributed across shards, for example userId or customerId, a text value with no units. It determines how evenly load is spread and which queries land on a single shard: a poor key creates a hot shard that hits its ceiling before the others.
shardStrategy: How a key maps to a shard: hash spreads data evenly but rules out range queries; range keeps neighboring keys together, which is handy for scans, though increasing keys create a hot range; directory uses an explicit lookup table, the most flexible option at the cost of an extra call. A dimensionless choice that determines how evenly load is spread.
shards: Number of shards (partitions) of the data or stream, as a count. It sets total capacity as the capacity of one shard × their number, along with the ceiling on consumer parallelism; changing it almost always requires a rebalance, so headroom is planned in advance.
shardsPerCore: How many shards there are per CPU core, as a count (1-4). The shard-per-core architecture is designed for 1: each core owns its own slice of data without locks, while a value above one introduces context switching and lowers efficiency.
shardsPerIndex: How many primary shards one index is split into, as a count (practical values 1-30). It sets the ceiling on search parallelism and the write volume per node; the rule of thumb is 10-50 GB per shard: small ones multiply coordination overhead, large ones cannot be split across nodes.
sharedDbConnections: Size of the shared database connection pool, as a count (1-5000, typically tens). A hard ceiling on the concurrency of database calls: 50 connections at 5 milliseconds per query give about 10000 requests per second, and everything above that waits in the pool, which shows up as a rise in p99.
showBoundBy: Display flag: whether to label which resource a block is bound by, CPU, memory, network or connections. It does not affect the calculation, but it tells you what to fix once utilization approaches the threshold.
showBytes: Display flag: whether to show traffic volume in bytes per second alongside the request count. It does not affect the calculation, but it is bytes rather than RPS that explain bandwidth saturation and egress cost.
showCacheMiss: Display flag: whether to highlight waterfall segments caused by a cache miss. It does not affect the calculation, it shows what share of the latency would disappear if the hit ratio grew.
showNetwork: Display flag: whether to show network latency between blocks as separate waterfall segments. It does not affect the calculation, but on cross-region calls it is the network, not the processing, that accounts for most of the time.
showQueueWait: Display flag: whether to separate queue wait from pure processing time on the histogram. It does not affect the calculation, it lets you tell whether p99 is rising because of slow code or because of overload.
showTimeToDrain: Display flag: whether to show the estimated time to drain the accumulated queue in seconds, that is depth divided by the consumer's spare capacity. It does not affect the calculation, but it answers the key question about lag, namely whether it will clear at all.
showWeakest: Display flag: whether to highlight the link with the lowest availability in the chain. It does not affect the calculation, and since a serial connection makes total availability the product, the weakest link is exactly what determines the result.
shuffleFactor: How many × the data volume pushed through shuffle between job stages exceeds the original input volume. A dimensionless multiplier, working range 1-5: it directly grows network traffic, temporary disk usage and job runtime.
signedUrls: Whether content is served only through signed URLs with a limited lifetime (yes/no). Enabling it protects private objects but adds signature verification at the edge, and if the signature is part of the cache key, hit ratio drops to nearly zero.
simulcastLayers: How many parallel versions of the same video stream at different bitrates the sender publishes, count (usually 1-3). Every extra layer multiplies the sender's uplink load and SFU CPU, but lets each receiver get a suitable quality without transcoding.
sizeMb: Capacity of the local in-process cache in megabytes. Together with the value size it determines how many keys fit, and through popularity skew it sets the achievable hit ratio and the residual load on the origin.
slaTier: Service requirement class of an internal consumer: critical - strict SLO and priority during degradation, standard - the usual level, best-effort - shed first under overload. It drives the target availability of the chain and whose traffic gets dropped first.
slabSizeKb: Size of a slab page in kilobytes, the chunks the allocator carves memory into for object classes; working range 512-8192 KB. Large slabs cut management overhead but increase internal fragmentation: if objects are much smaller than the slab, part of the memory is wasted.
slotCount: Number of slots - units of parallel compute available to analytical queries, count. Working range 500-20000: slots directly set throughput and cost, and when they run short queries queue up instead of simply slowing down proportionally.
slowConsumerShare: A share from 0 to 1 of subscribers that respond slowly or with errors; typically 0.01-0.2. Such receivers tie up delivery workers and grow the retry queue disproportionately to their share, so even 5 percent can eat most of the pool.
snapshotMode: How the connector captures the source's initial state before streaming changes: never - new changes only, schema-only - take the DDL alone, initial - one full snapshot on first start, always - a snapshot on every restart. Full snapshots cause a one-off load spike on the source and a large volume of traffic.
softCommitMs: Soft commit interval in milliseconds after which new documents become visible to search; working range 500-15000 milliseconds. A lower value keeps the index fresher but opens segments and drops caches more often, which hurts search p99.
sortKey: Sort key scheme that defines the physical order of rows: none - unsorted, compound - by a column prefix, interleaved - with equal weight for all columns. A good key lets scans skip blocks and cuts query time and cost, while interleaved is more expensive to maintain.
sourceDb: Type of the source database changes are captured from: postgres, mysql, mongodb or sqlserver. It determines the capture mechanism (logical replication and WAL, binlog, oplog, transaction log) and with it the log retention limits and the extra load on the source.
sourceMinutes: Duration of the source media file in minutes, typically 1-120. Together with the processing speed it sets the machine time for transcoding, and together with the number of output profiles it sets the volume of finished renditions in storage.
spanBytes: Average size of a single span in bytes after serialization, including attributes and events; typically 500-1500 bytes. Multiplied by the number of spans and by RPS, this is exactly the data stream into the tracing system and its storage volume.
spansPerRequest: How many spans a single incoming request produces, count; typically 5-60. A direct multiplier of telemetry volume: deep microservice chains with retries easily exceed a hundred spans per request.
speedFactor: How many × faster processing runs than the real time of the content: 1 - a minute of video per minute of compute, 4 - four times faster. A dimensionless multiplier (realistically 0.3-20) that divides the source duration to give processing time and the required number of workers.
spikeFactor: How many × a scheduled run raises instantaneous RPS above the background level; typically 2-50. A dimensionless multiplier: cron jobs fire in bursts, so downstream capacity must be sized on the peak rather than on the period average.
splitByFlow: Whether to break the measured RPS down by individual traffic flows instead of a single aggregate figure (yes/no). It affects only the granularity of the probe report; the load itself and the calculation do not change.
splitByOperation: Whether to show RPS separately per operation type - read, write, search - instead of one total (yes/no). It affects only the granularity of the probe output, but it helps see which class of operations is hitting the ceiling.
staleWhileRevalidateSec: How many seconds after TTL expiry the cache keeps serving the stale object while refreshing it in the background. A non-zero value (usually 30-300 seconds) removes the miss spike at the TTL boundary and shields the origin from stampede at the cost of a slightly outdated response.
stampedeProtection: Cache stampede protection: on a miss only one request goes to the origin and the rest wait for its result (yes/no). Enabling it cuts the peak backend load at the moment a popular key expires, adding only one origin round-trip of waiting.
startupSec: Cold start time of an instance in seconds until it is ready to take traffic. It sets autoscaling inertia and the depth of the capacity dip during a rollout or restart: at 90 seconds the reaction to a spike arrives no sooner than a minute and a half later.
stateSizeGb: Size of the job state in gigabytes - windows, join buffers and aggregates held by the state store. It determines worker memory and disk, checkpoint size and recovery time after a failure, so a large state stretches recovery several times over.
stateStore: Where the state of running workflows is kept: database - transactional and durable but costlier in latency, redis - fast but with a risk of loss, kafka - an event log with replay. The choice sets the latency of a single saga step and the behaviour when the orchestrator recovers from a crash.
stepsPerWorkflow: How many steps, including compensating ones, a single saga contains, count; typically 3-30. A load multiplier: each step is a state write plus a participant call, so 8 steps at 2000 workflows per second already means 16000 operations per second.
stickiness: How the load balancer pins a client to a backend: none - free distribution, source-ip - by client address, flow-hash - by the connection 5-tuple. Pinning helps local caches and sessions, but it worsens load evenness and makes draining a node more painful.
stickyReadShare: A share from 0 to 1 of reads that must go to the primary for read-your-writes and cannot be offloaded to replicas. The higher the value, the smaller the benefit from read replicas and the sooner the primary hits its CPU and IOPS ceiling.
stickyRegion: Whether to pin a user to a single region for the whole session instead of routing by proximity and health (yes/no). Enabling it preserves the consistency of session data but slows failover and can leave a user on a distant region with higher RTT for a long time.
storageClass: Object storage class: standard - hot data, infrequent-access - cheaper per GB but charged for every access, glacier - archive with the lowest price and minutes to hours to restore. It directly sets storage cost per GB and the time to first byte on read.
storageGb: Total data volume in storage in gigabytes, including indexes but excluding replicas and backups. The baseline figure for storage cost and for estimating how much of the data can fit into memory or cache at all.
storageGbPerNode: How many gigabytes of data sit on one cluster node. Together with the total volume and the replication factor it sets the required node count: higher density means cheaper hardware but longer rebuild and rebalance when a node is lost.
storageOverhead: How many × more raw disk capacity is needed than useful data once erasure coding and headroom are counted - a dimensionless multiplier from 1 to 4. A value of 1.5 roughly matches an EC 8+4 scheme and multiplies hardware cost directly.
strategy: ID issuing algorithm: snowflake - timestamp plus node id, generated locally, uuidv7 - 128 bits, time-sortable and coordination-free, ticket-server - a centralized counter with a network round-trip. It affects generation latency, key size and the locality of index inserts.
streamRetention: Message retention policy for the stream: limits - keep up to the age and size limits, interest - while interested subscribers exist, workqueue - delete right after a single consumer processes the message. It determines storage volume and whether history can be re-read.
streams: Whether to enable the table's change stream for downstream subscribers (yes/no). Enabling it writes every modification into a separate log - extra storage volume and cost - but lets CDC work without polling the table.
subjects: Number of distinct subjects - routing topics - in the system, count. It affects routing table size and subscription granularity: hundreds of subjects are free, tens of thousands noticeably load routing and metadata.
subrequestsPerInvocation: How many outgoing HTTP calls the function makes per invocation, count (0 - it answers entirely on its own). A traffic multiplier onto the origin and external APIs, and a direct addition to execution time and per-invocation cost.
subscribers: How many receivers are subscribed to a single event, count; typically from 2 to a few dozen. The key fanout multiplier: one publish turns into that many deliveries, retries and outbound connections, so the outbound load is a multiple of this number.
subscriptionType: Subscription model: exclusive - a single consumer, failover - a standby takes over on failure, shared - round-robin across a group with no ordering, key-shared - parallel but ordered within a key. It determines the achievable read parallelism and the ordering guarantees.
synchronous: How strictly the engine fsyncs on commit: off - do not wait for the disk (fast, but data is lost on power failure), normal - a compromise combined with WAL, full - a guaranteed write to the medium. It directly sets commit latency - from a fraction of a millisecond to a few milliseconds - and the durability level.
tailSampling: Whether to decide a trace's fate after it completes, based on errors and latency, instead of sampling randomly at ingest (yes/no). Enabling it keeps almost every interesting trace at a low storage share, but it requires buffering all spans in the collector - memory plus extra export delay.
targetAvailability: Target availability as a share from 0 to 1: 0.999 is three nines, about 43 minutes of downtime per month. The probe compares the chain's computed availability against it and reports the error budget left for the window.
targetP99Ms: Target p99 latency bound in milliseconds that the SLO probe checks. The route's computed p99 is compared against this number: exceeding it is flagged as an SLO violation and burns error budget.
targetRps: Target load of the load-test client in requests per second. This synthetic traffic adds to normal user traffic, so the system must be validated against the sum rather than against the test alone.
threads: Number of worker threads serving network connections, count; working range 4-16. It sets the node's throughput in operations, but above 8-16 threads the bottleneck usually shifts to the network and interrupts rather than CPU.
throughputGbps: Throughput of a node or device in gigabits per second. A hard traffic ceiling: as the aggregate data flow approaches it, queueing and latency grow and extra instances are needed.
throughputMbPerCoreSec: How many megabytes of input data one core processes per second; typically 2-50 MB/s depending on the format and the complexity of the transformations. The job volume divided by this value and by the core count gives the runtime.
throughputMbs: Maximum storage throughput in megabytes per second. It caps read and write speed: as the ceiling is approached, requests queue up and latency grows non-linearly.
throughputMbsPerBroker: How many megabytes per second a single broker sustains across writes, replication and consumer reads; realistically 100-500 MB/s per node with NVMe. The total topic flow divided by this value gives the minimum broker count.
throughputMbsPerNode: Throughput of a single data node in megabytes per second; realistically 100-2000 MB/s. The bandwidth of the whole cluster equals this value times the node count, and it caps how fast a full dataset scan can run.
throughputMultiplier: How many × more operations a node sustains than a comparable node on a JVM engine, thanks to shard-per-core and the absence of GC pauses. A dimensionless capacity multiplier, realistically 3-5: it divides the required cluster node count.
throughputPerGpu: How many inference requests per second a single GPU serves for the given model and batch size; realistically 5-5000 depending on the model. The target RPS divided by this value gives the accelerator count and the main cost item.
throughputPerPrefixMbs: Throughput per key prefix in megabytes per second. Object storage shards load by prefix, so all traffic aimed at one prefix will hit this ceiling regardless of bucket size - keys need to be spread out.
throughputPerQueue: How many messages per second a single queue sustains, requests per second; realistically 20000-50000. A queue is the unit of parallelism, and past that ceiling only splitting into several queues or shards helps, not beefier hardware.
tieredOffloadHours: After how many hours segments are offloaded from broker disks to object storage; typically 1-168 hours. A lower value means cheaper storage and relieved brokers, but reads of older data come from object storage and are noticeably slower.
tieredStorage: Whether to move old segments to cheap object storage instead of local broker disks (yes/no). Enabling it makes long retention far cheaper and takes load off broker disks at the cost of higher latency when reading history.
timeoutMs: How many milliseconds to wait for a response before aborting the call and counting it as failed. The timeout should be well above the downstream p99 but below the caller's timeout: too large holds workers and builds a queue, too small breeds retries and extra load.
tlsHandshakeMs: CPU cost of a TLS handshake in milliseconds per new connection. It counts only for new connections, so with a low keep-alive share it becomes a noticeable part of CPU load and an addition to the latency of the first request.
tlsHandshakeRtt: How many network round-trips are needed to establish a TLS session, count: TLS 1.3 - 1, TLS 1.2 - 2, 0 with resumption and 0-RTT. It is multiplied by the link RTT and added to the latency of the first request on a connection.
tlsTerminate: Whether to terminate TLS at the load balancer or pass traffic straight through to the backend (yes/no). Termination unlocks L7 routing and takes crypto off the services, but it moves the cost of handshakes and encryption onto the balancer itself.
tokenTtlSec: Lifetime of an issued access token in seconds. A short TTL revokes access faster but multiplies the stream of refresh requests to the auth service: 900 seconds is a common compromise between security and load.
tombstoneRatio: A share from 0 to 1 of deleted records (tombstones) among the rows being read. Before compaction tombstones are read alongside live data, so a share above 0.1 directly raises read latency and on-disk volume.
topHops: How many route hops to show in the latency waterfall breakdown, count. It affects only the granularity of the probe report: a longer list exposes small contributions but makes the dominant one harder to spot.
topK: How many nearest neighbours the search returns per query, count; working range 5-100. A larger K means more candidates traversed in HNSW or IVF and higher query latency at roughly the same index size.
topN: How many of the busiest flows or nodes to list in the probe report, count. It affects only the granularity of the output and does not change the traffic calculation.
topics: Number of topics in the cluster, count. Together with the partitions per topic it gives the total partition count, and that means open files, metadata volume and controller load during rebalancing.
transactionScope: Scope of a typical transaction: none, single-row, single-shard, cross-shard or distributed-2pc. The wider the scope, the more participants and coordination rounds - a direct addition to write latency and a higher chance of conflicts and retries.
traversalDepth: How many edge hops a typical graph traversal covers, count; working range 1-4. Cost grows roughly exponentially in the average vertex degree, so a depth of 3-4 already visits thousands of nodes per query.
trueTimeUncertaintyMs: Uncertainty window of the global clock in milliseconds, realistically 1-7 ms. Committing an externally consistent transaction waits out this window, so the value is added directly to the latency of every write.
ttlDays: How many days data lives in the table before it is deleted automatically or moved to a cold tier. Multiplied by the daily data intake, this is exactly the resulting storage volume and its cost.
ttlEnabled: Whether automatic deletion of expired records is enabled (yes/no). Enabling it keeps table growth in check, but the background deletes consume write capacity themselves and the cleanup is not instant - the delay can reach several hours.
ttlSec: Lifetime of a cache entry in seconds: once it expires the entry counts as stale and must be refreshed from the origin. A longer TTL means a higher hit ratio and less backend load, but a higher risk of serving outdated data.
typoTolerance: Whether to tolerate typos in the search query, that is fuzzy matching by Levenshtein distance (yes/no). Enabling it noticeably improves recall on real queries, but it widens the index traversal and raises search latency.
uniqueKeys: How many distinct keys exist in the dataset in total, count. Together with the value size it gives the required memory, and paired with cache capacity and popularity skew it gives the achievable hit ratio.
updateLagMin: How many minutes after a data change the suggestions are updated; typically 1-60 minutes. A larger lag means less frequent index rebuilds and cheaper maintenance, but suggestions visibly trail the real state of the data.
updatesPerSec: How many coordinate updates per second the geo index accepts, requests per second. Writes to a spatial index cost more than reads, so this is the main driver of CPU load and of the need for sharding.
usableTb: Usable capacity of the cluster available to the application in terabytes - already net of erasure coding and headroom. Together with the overhead multiplier it gives the raw disk capacity and the hardware cost.
vacuumNeeded: Whether a periodic VACUUM with re-sorting is required after bulk loads and deletes (yes/no). The maintenance takes a share of the cluster's compute capacity, but without it the fraction of unsorted and deleted blocks grows and scans gradually slow down.
valueSizeBytes: Average size of a single stored value in bytes, excluding the key and service headers. Multiplied by the number of keys it gives the required memory; with large values the bottleneck becomes network bandwidth rather than the operation count.
varyHeaders: How many request headers take part in the cache key through Vary, count; keep it at 0-3. Each extra header multiplies the number of variants of the same object and cuts hit ratio accordingly.
vectorCount: How many vectors are stored in the index, count. Together with dimensionality it sets the memory needed for HNSW or IVF and the traversal depth during search, so it determines both cost and query latency.
verifyMs: Time to verify a token or session in milliseconds per request. Local signature verification takes a fraction of a millisecond, a call to an external store takes a few milliseconds, and this figure is added to every single request without exception.
versioning: Whether to keep previous object versions on overwrite and delete (yes/no). Enabling it protects against accidental loss, but storage grows by the sum of all versions, so lifecycle cleanup rules are mandatory.
visibilityTimeoutSec: How many seconds a message stays hidden from other consumers after it is received, while processing runs. The value must exceed the real processing time: too short and the message gets processed twice, too long and it hangs invisible for ages if the worker dies.
volumeType: Block volume type: gp3 - general purpose with a baseline IOPS level, io2 - guaranteed high IOPS and low latency jitter, nvme - a local disk with minimal latency but no data durability when the instance stops. It determines the achievable IOPS, latency and cost per gigabyte.
vtgateInstances: How many vtgate proxy instances sit in front of the shards, count. Total proxy capacity equals this number times the RPS of one instance; fewer than two instances means no fault tolerance.
vtgateLatencyMs: Overhead latency of the proxy layer in milliseconds added to every query on top of the shard's own time; realistically 0.2-2 ms. For scatter queries across many shards the contribution is noticeably higher, since the proxy waits for the slowest shard.
vtgateMaxRps: How many requests per second a single proxy instance sustains, requests per second; working range 5000-50000. The target RPS divided by this value gives the minimum number of vtgate instances.
walRetentionGb: How many gigabytes of transaction log (WAL or binlog) the source retains for a lagging connector. Too small a buffer risks the slot being dropped when the consumer stops, forcing a full re-snapshot; too large risks filling the source's disk.
warehouseSize: Size of the compute cluster: each step from x-small to x-large roughly doubles the node count, and therefore both query speed and hourly cost. For a linearly scalable query the price per query barely changes - the choice mainly affects response time.
warmupSec: How many seconds it takes to warm an instance up - loading weights into accelerator memory, compiling the graph, the first batches - before it reaches full speed. It sets autoscaling inertia: during a spike, new capacity only really appears after this time.
warnThreshold: The utilization level rho, a share from 0 to 1, at which the probe flags a node as approaching its limit. 0.7 is the customary threshold: beyond it the queueing formula makes latency and p99 grow much faster than the load itself.
watchers: How many concurrent watch subscriptions on key changes the cluster holds, count. Every change is broadcast to all matching watchers, so this means both memory for connections and sharp spikes of outbound traffic during mass updates.
watermarkLagSec: How far in seconds the watermark trails current time, that is how long late events are awaited before a window closes; typically 1-300 seconds. A larger lag gives more complete and accurate results, but higher end-to-end latency and more state held in memory.
wcu: How many write units per second are provisioned for the table; one WCU is one write of up to 1 KB per second. Exceeding it leads to throttling and retries, and the value itself directly determines the table's cost.
webhookCallback: Whether the external provider reports the result asynchronously, via a callback to our endpoint, instead of making us wait in a synchronous response (yes/no). Enabling it removes long-held connections and workers, but it requires a public receiver, idempotency and handling of duplicate deliveries.
windowDays: Length of the window in days over which availability and error budget are computed; 30 days is the standard. The shorter the window, the more sharply the metric reacts to a single incident - and the faster that incident drops out of it.
windowHours: How many hours the batch job must finish within - the processing window; typically 0.5-12 hours. The data volume is divided by this window: a narrow window needs proportionally more cores, a wide one is cheaper but the result is less fresh.
windowSec: Averaging interval in seconds over which the probe computes RPS. A short window shows spikes, a long one smooths them out: 300 seconds completely hides the second-scale peaks that capacity should actually be sized on.
windowType: Aggregation window type: tumbling - non-overlapping intervals, sliding - overlapping, where an event lands in several windows at once, session - split by pauses in user activity. Sliding and session multiply state size and computation cost compared with tumbling.
wiredTigerCacheGb: How many gigabytes of RAM are given to the storage engine cache. If the working set does not fit into it, reads go to disk and latency grows by an order of magnitude; usually about half of the node's RAM is allocated.
workers: Number of workers in the distributed query cluster, count; working range 2-200. It directly sets scan parallelism and cost: query time falls roughly inversely with the worker count until the data source becomes the bottleneck.
workflowsPerSec: How many sagas or workflows start per second, requests per second. Multiplied by the number of steps in each, it gives the real load on the orchestrator and its state store, which is usually an order of magnitude higher than this figure itself.
workingSetGb: Volume of hot data in gigabytes that queries actually touch, as opposed to the total stored volume. If the working set fits into the buffer pool or cache, reads come from memory; if not, you fall back to disk IOPS with latency an order of magnitude higher.
writeAmplification: How many × the data actually written to disk exceeds the logical write volume, because of compaction and SSTable rewrites. A dimensionless multiplier, typically 2-6 for LSM engines: it consumes disk IOPS and bandwidth directly, capping write intake.
writeConcern: How many nodes must acknowledge a write: w1 - the primary only (fast, but data can be lost on failover), majority - most replicas, all - every node. Each higher level adds a round-trip to the slowest required replica to write latency.
writeQuorumMs: Time to reach Raft quorum for one write in milliseconds, including the leader's fsync and majority acknowledgement; realistically 5-50 ms within a single data centre. This is the lower bound on the latency of any write, and stretching the cluster across regions pushes it to hundreds of milliseconds.
writeRegion: Identifier of the region that accepts writes in a single-writer setup, for example eu-west-1 (text value; empty - no region pinned). Writes from the other regions travel here over the cross-region link, adding a full inter-region RTT to latency.
writeServiceMs: Pure service time of one write operation on the storage side in milliseconds, excluding network latency and queue waiting. Its reciprocal is the ceiling of operations per connection or worker: 2 ms of service time yields about 500 writes per second.
writesPerTransaction: How many write operations are batched into one transaction, count; working range 1-1000. Batching amortizes the expensive fsync on commit and multiplies throughput, but on failure the entire batch is lost or rolled back as a whole.
zipfAlpha: The alpha exponent of the Zipf distribution describing key popularity skew - a dimensionless value, realistically 0.6-1.4. The higher it is, the more traffic concentrates on a few hot keys and the higher the hit ratio at the same cache size.
hitRatioMode: Where the cache hit ratio comes from: "Auto" — the model computes it from the key count, cache size, the Zipf distribution and TTL; "Manual" — the declared number is used. A dimensionless choice; auto reacts to parameter changes, while a manual value stays what you set and therefore fits when the ratio is known from observation.
hitRatioOverride: The hit ratio used instead of the computed one when the hit ratio mode is set to "Manual" (0-1). A value of 0.9 means only every tenth read reaches the store.
